g/m2-s for normal flames, and an oxygen-based mass flux of 0.68 g/m2-s for inverse flames. With this information, we

atmospheric-pressure ethylene spherical diffusion flame given only the reactant mass flow rate. Flame growth, which
ultimately leads to radiative extinction if the critical extinction point is reached, is attributed to the natural development
of the diffusion limited system as it approaches steady state and the reduction in the transport properties as the flame
temperature drops due to increasing flame radiation with time (radiation-induced growth).

Our work on the numerical model has continued. We have run multiple cases with the University of California San
Diego (UCSD) mechanism. We continue to investigate the boundary conditions for radiation and conduction. Because
burner heating can significantly affect the flame diameter and lifetime, we have started to implement a heat balance at
the burner surface to solve for burner temperature and better conserve enthalpy. We simulated ethylene flames to
perform parametric studies in an attempt to find conditions that are favorable to steady state flames. We compared the
simulation results with experimental results. Work is underway to update the globally implicit solver to the
time-splitting method. We modified the SphDiff code to plot the radius of stoichiometric mixture fraction as a function
of time, both for non-reacting and reacting flows. We added 2nd order upwind scheme. We modified the transient term
in the conservation of mass

time, both for non-reacting and reacting flows. We added 2nd order upwind scheme. We modified the transient term
in the conservation of mass equation so that it captures the density change due to temperature and concentration
changes. We added an automatic temperature initialization scheme from an analytical droplet combustion model.

investigated in the literature and in the laboratory. Additional published flame lengths were added to our draft paper on

double luminous zones was made at ASGSR (American Society for Gravitational & Space Research) in Seattle.
At UMD we tested IDFs (inverse diffusion flames) with CO2 as diluent in both fuel side and oxidizer side. These did not

|W. Wu, G. Yablonsky, R.L. Axelbaum, Observation of Water-Gas Shift Equilibrium in Diffusion Flames, Combustion
and Flame, accepted. The kinetic behavior of the water-gas-shift (WGS) sub-system has been studied computationally

from equilibrium. Two scenarios were observed for WGS equilibrium:
(1) Full equilibrium in which every step of the WGS-mechanism is nearly in equilibrium;|

|(2) “Apparent” equilibrium, which is achieved via opposing but coherent shifts away from equilibrium for the two key
elementary reactions that constitute the WGS reaction. This interesting phenomenon is caused by the supply of the H
radical, which participates in the forward reaction of one step and the reverse reaction of the other. This new form of
apparent equilibrium differs from well-known “quasi” equilibrium, which is typically caused by the combination of a
fast reversible step and slow irreversible step.|

||The predictions of the Roper model are compared with the measured flame lengths. For normal flames the agreement is

simplified model predicts flame length from the methane flow rate and mole fraction and the oxygen mole fraction.|

flames fueled by gases. Its emphasis is on soot formation and flame extinction. This experiment, and associated
ground-based work, attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within the inherent
constraints, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants. This presentation will introduce the
overall concepts of Flame Design. It will summarize observations in the NASA Glenn 2.2 s and 5 s drop facilities,
which have yielded important insights into soot formation and flame extinction behavior.

the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.

ambient reactant for both normal and inverse flames

diffusion flames except for the smallest burners with radii on the order of 1 micron. At high flow rates
H+OH(+M)?H2O(+M) contributes over 40% of the net heat release. However at flow rates approaching quenching
limits, H+O2(+M)?HO2(+M) is the elementary reaction with the largest heat release rate. The corresponding author for

|**Task Description:**|The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial performance
penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these concerns. The
approach is termed “Flame Design” as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames and, within
the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize pollutants.

|The following is a summary of the research activities during the period Oct. 2006 - Sept. 2009.
1) Numerical and Experimental Observations of Spherical Diffusion Flames. Spherical diffusion flames supported on a

||The overwhelming majority of practical combustion processes involve non-premixed combustion of hydrocarbons.
These processes must be efficient and the resulting emissions low. For example, soot production, which can adversely
affect efficiency, emissions, and equipment lifetime, must be controlled, and flame extinction must be avoided. Many
methods have been considered to reduce soot, such as increasing strain rates and inert concentrations and reducing
pressures, but these techniques generally weaken the flame, leading to extinction and resulting in substantial
performance penalties. The proposed study considers a novel method of approaching combustion to address these
concerns. The approach is termed 'Flame Design' as it attempts to take our fundamental understanding of diffusion flames
and, within the inherent constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize
pollutants. Recognizing the unique benefits of

constraints imposed on the problem, design flames that best optimize efficiency and minimize
pollutants. Recognizing the unique benefits of spherical diffusion flames, employ such flames to:
1. Obtain soot-inception limits as functions of stoichiometric mixture fraction, flow direction (direction across the flame
front, i.e., towards the fuel or towards the oxidizer), amount of inert (nitrogen) and pressure for ethylene and methane
flames. Identify the corresponding soot-inception temperature;|

|---|---| |**Task Description:**|2. Determine effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on the phenomenon of permanently blue
flames and, to this end, determine the effects of stoichiometric mixture fraction and flow direction on flame
temperature, size, color and soot volume fraction;|

**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)**

**PURPOSE:** ACME is focused on advanced combustion technology via fundamental microgravity research. The primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion.  A secondary objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.  
_U.S. astronaut Christina Koch preparing the ACME chamber insert for the Flame Design experiment._  
**RESEARCH:** ACME includes six independent experiments investigating laminar and nonpremixed flames of gaseous fuels. The experiments are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). While the ISS astronauts set up the experimental hardware, the ACME tests are remotely commanded from the NASA Glenn Research Center.  
_Canadian astronaut David Saint-Jacques replacing the igniter tip on the ACME chamber insert._  
_Example images from ACME’s Flame Design experiment._
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)**

_Example images from ACME’s Flame Design experiment._  
**STATUS:** ACME was set up by the ISS crew in September and October 2017 where thus far 21 astronauts from Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia, and the United States have supported the project’s research. Over 800 flames have been ignited since November 2017 for five of the six ACME experiments. On-orbit testing has yet to begin for the CFIG experiment. In contrast, the planned testing for the E–FIELD Flames investigation has been completed. Testing is currently underway for the s–Flame experiment. ACME tests are expected to continue on the ISS through most, if not all, of 2020.  
_U.S. astronaut Joe Acaba and Russian cosmonaut Alexander Misurkin exchanging a CIR oxidizer bottle._

What Is Microgravity?

Gravity is a force that governs motion throughout the universe. It holds us to the ground and keeps the Earth in orbit around the Sun. Microgravity describes the environment in orbital space flight, which has very weak gravitational effects (one-millionth of what is felt on Earth) and which is sometimes referred to as a state of “weightlessness.” The condition of microgravity occurs when an object is in “free fall.” In free fall, an object falls faster and faster, accelerating with exactly the speed of attraction caused by gravity. Objects travelling around the Earth in a state of continuous free fall, or orbit, are essentially weightless even though their mass remains the same.
**Unlocking Mysteries in Microgravity:** NASA Glenn Provides the Keys With the Fluids and Combustion Facility
What Is Microgravity?

Conducting research in a microgravity environment gives researchers a unique opportunity to study the true nature of processes and materials without having to consider the effects of Earth’s gravity. Thus, physics theories can be tested at levels of accuracy that are impossible on Earth. Microgravity experiments uncover the mystery of how gravity affects processes such as combustion science and fluid physics. This knowledge can then help to improve the way we do things on Earth.

A World-Class Orbiting Laboratory

The term “microgravity” will become more commonplace when the International Space Station (ISS) is fully operational. The ISS will be the largest orbiting space structure and the largest international scientific and technological endeavor in history. Sixteen countries, including the United States, are participating in this record-breaking project. The ISS is a permanent laboratory in space where studies can be performed without the effects of gravity.  
The space station provides researchers with all the laboratory space and equipment and electrical power needed for safe, long-term research by human beings in space. The ISS enables larger and longer experiments than were possible on the typical 2-week space shuttle mission. This gives scientists time for more detailed observation in the microgravity environment.

Combustion Science

Combustion, or burning, is a process in which a substance reacts with oxygen to give off heat and light. Combustion meets almost 85 percent of the U.S. energy needs. While it does a good job of powering how we live on Earth, combustion is a major contributor to air pollution.  
The cost of combustion energy is about $450 billion each year in the United States. In any area of the economy where a huge amount of money is spent, even the smallest improvements in efficiency can mean savings of very large amounts of money. A mere 1 percent increase in fuel efficiency, like improving your gas mileage from 25 miles per gallon to 25.25 miles per gallon, would translate into a savings to America of nearly 100 million barrels of oil a year (roughly $5.5 million per day at today’s cost). Although today combustion is vital to transportation, materials processing, hazardous waste disposal, and many other areas, there is still only limited understanding of many of its fundamental characteristics.

Fluid Physics

Of the four states of matter—solid, liquid, gas, and plasma—three are fluid, meaning they flow in response to an applied force. An understanding of fluid physics is not only vital to advancing aircraft and spacecraft applications, such as airflow and propellant management, but is also essential to understanding the human body, aspects of everyday life, and many industrial processes. In microgravity, fluid positioning and flow characteristics can be studied from a new perspective.

Fluid Physics

Scientists at NASA Glenn Research Center have played an important role in fluid physics research since the 1940s. With orbiting spacecraft, microgravity fluid physics became an important research area in which NASA Glenn has always played a leading role. Glenn is currently focusing its research on the enabling technology for space exploration (water and fuel flow, life support systems, temperature control, etc.) as well as on using the space environment (reduced gravity) to provide insight into phenomena that are important for Earth-based applications. One spinoff of the special nonintrusive instruments and techniques developed to perform the fluid experiments is a dynamic light scattering (DLS) probe and Hruby lens holder that make early detection of cataracts and other eye diagnoses easier.

Fluid Physics

Glenn researchers have also experimented with the behavior of colloidal suspensions. A colloid is a system of fine particles suspended in a fluid. Italian salad dressing provides a simple illustration of the effects of microgravity on the behavior of colloidal suspensions. In space you would need to shake the dressing only once, rather than between uses, which is needed on Earth. Paint, ink, milk, and orange juice are also common examples. Though these products are routinely produced and used, scientists know little about the underlying structure of colloidal systems because they are difficult to study in ground-based laboratories. Understanding their structures may allow scientists to manipulate the physical properties of colloids for the creation of new materials and products or to improve the manufacturing of known products.

Experiments by Remote Control

While the astronauts perform their roles in experiment setup, operation, observation, evaluation, and feedback, the FCF is teleoperated from the NASA Glenn Research Center. Operation of experiments via remote control is coordinated through the Telescience Support Center (TSC) at Glenn. Telescience is the systematic monitoring, command, and control of an experiment from a remote location and has already been implemented successfully by NASA on the shuttle/Spacelab and the Russian Mir Space Station. In concert with the work performed by the astronauts in space and the Cleveland-based operations team, the FCF principle investigator’s (PI’s) experiment can remotely monitor and control from the PI’s home site through Glenn’s TSC.

**_Telescience Support Center._**  
The concept of telescience offers several advantages. Typically, the development of an experiment takes years and involves a varied group of scientists, engineers, and support personnel. Only a few of these people need to be on the operations team that travels to a NASA center to support actual mission operations. A major benefit of remote operations is that the entire team that developed and built the experiment can be connected to the operations team to support data analysis, command decisions, anomaly resolution, and other real-time considerations. Also, some facilities that are not physically located at NASA centers can be included (e.g., colleges, universities, and industrial labs). Additional benefits are reductions in travel requirements and increases in the amount of science data acquired.

**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)**

**PURPOSE:** ACME is focused on advanced combustion technology via fundamental microgravity research. The primary goal is to improve efficiency and reduce pollutant emission in practical terrestrial combustion. A secondary objective is fire prevention, especially for spacecraft.  
_German astronaut Alex Gerst exchanging the nitrogen mass flow controller on the ACME chamber insert within the CIR facility._  
**RESEARCH:** ACME includes six independent experiments investigating laminar, nonpremixed flames of gaseous fuels. The experiments are being conducted with a single set of modular hardware in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS). While the ISS astronauts set up the experimental hardware, the ACME tests are remotely commanded from NASA’s Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center.  
_Example flame from the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment led by Prof. Jim Quintiere (University of Maryland)._
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME)**

_Example flame from the Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment led by Prof. Jim Quintiere (University of Maryland)._  
_U.S. astronaut Joe Acaba and Russian cosmonaut Alexander Misurkin exchanging the CIR oxidizer bottle._  
**STATUS:** ACME was setup by the ISS crew in Sept.-Oct. 2017 where thus far sixteen astronauts from Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan, Russia, and the United States have supported the research.  Since November 2017, over 550 flames have been ignited for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame), Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames), and Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiments. They are respectively led by Profs. Marshall Long (Yale University), Derek Dunn-Rankin (University of California, Irvine), and Jim Quintiere (University of Maryland).  Russian collaborators on those experiments are with the Far Eastern Federal University and Peter the Great St. Petersburg Polytechnic University.

**I. Introduction**

The Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment was conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  In this experiment, an electric field with voltages as high as 10,000 volts was established between the burner and a flat, circular mesh electrode suspended above (i.e., downstream of) the burner.  The motion of the charged ions, which are naturally produced within the flame, are strongly affected by a strong electric field.  The resulting ion-driven wind can dramatically influence the stability and sooting behavior of the flame.  Measurements were made of electric-field strength, the ion current passing through the flame, and flame characteristics such as the size, structure, temperature, soot, and stability.  Conducting the tests in microgravity allowed for great simplifications in the analysis of ion-driven convection and flame

**I. Introduction**

An electric field can strongly influence flames because of its effect on the ions produced as a result of the combustion reactions. The induced ion wind can modify the flame shape, alter the soot and stability limits, and direct the heat transfer.  The purpose of the E-FIELD Flames experiment is to gain an improved understanding of flame ion production and learn how the electric field can be used to manipulate the ions and control non-premixed flames for practical benefit.  For example, electric fields can enable stable burner operation at fuel-lean conditions with reduced pollutant emission, i.e., where the flame is not reliably sustained without the electric field.  As another example, the role of electric fields on soot formation can be dramatic. It appears that the ion driven wind alters the local convection and strongly influences the residence time of the soot precursors within the hot flame.  The experiment contributes to our critical understanding of combustion processes in

**I. Introduction**

More specifically, E-FIELD Flames has the following experimental objectives:  
- A. Determine the relationship between electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and the amount of inert (nitrogen) in the fuel.  
- B. Obtain the time response of the flame chemiluminescence, luminosity, and the ion current to large step changes in voltage, as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.  
- C. Evaluate and manipulate sooting behavior (i.e., soot volume fraction and location of luminous soot) in relation to the electric field voltage and chemi-ion current as functions of total fuel (methane and ethylene) flow rate and amount of inert (nitrogen) added to the fuel stream.
**I. Introduction**

- D. Use the variation of the chemi-ion current as a function of applied voltage to characterize the combustion behavior of near-limit lifted flames and use the associated ion-driven wind to stabilize or reattach these flames.
**I. Introduction**

The effect of the electric field on the flame is studied through tests conducted with a range of flame and electric field conditions.  The fuel, fuel jet velocity, air flow, electric-field voltage and polarity were the primary parameters of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  Tests were conducted with methane and ethylene, including nitrogen dilutions of each, which provide a broad range of soot-producing conditions, i.e., from soot-free to highly sooting.  They were carried out with both a simple gas-jet burner and the coflow burner that was also used for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment.  Tests with the coflow burner were conducted with and without a coflow of air, where the results of the latter are compared with those from the gas-jet burner to assess the effect of air entrainment on the flame.  The coflow burner also provided a different electrode configuration (close to a plane-to-plane) than the jet burner (close to a point-to-plane). In a typical test, the

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancy-

driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Therefore, the flicker in the E-FIELD Flames was a result of electric body forces alone.  Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application.
**II. Methods/Research Operations**
**A. Discussion of Method/Protocol**

E-FIELD Flames and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.
**II. Methods/Research Operations**
**A. Discussion of Method/Protocol**

All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.  For example, the mesh voltage can be adjusted to approach a flame’s stability or soot limit.  This was not done during Increments 55-56 or 57-58, where the console commanding during a test was typically limited to halting the test when it was observed in the analog ops video that the flame had extinguished.  
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.

**III. Results**
**A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight**

A total of 219 flames were ignited for the E-FIELD Flames experiment, with 142 and 77 respectively ignited during Increments 55-56 and 57-58.  Note that the investigation’s testing was completed during Increment 57, so no flames were ignited during Increment 58.  The first and second rounds of testing respectively occurred in March-May 2018 and September-November 2018.  The two rounds of tests resulted in 120 and 99 ignited flames conducted with coflow and gas-jet burners, respectively.  The coflow burner was developed for the Coflow Laminar Diffusion Flame (CLD Flame) experiment, where CLD Flames’ second round occurred between the two rounds of the E-FIELD Flames experiment.  The ‘interruption’ in the E-FIELD Flames testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.
**III. Results**
**A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight**

E-FIELD Flames does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene. Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond.  For both fuels, tests were conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen over a broad range of dilutions.  For limited cases, the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch.  ACME bottles were launched with methane concentrations of 30%, 40%, 45%, and 100% with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  Similarly, bottles were launched with ethylene concentrations of 30%, 50%, and 100%, again with a balance of nitrogen (on a volume basis).  But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous

E-FIELD Flames tests sometimes automatically aborted (due to the controlling software script), where that was typically prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter.  As a result, there was little lost other than the time in the failed test attempt. The aborts normally occurred because of communication issues with IPSU-1. **III. Results**
**B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies**

Tests are of course also unsuccessful when the flame fails to ignite.  The first test of the day has sometimes failed to ignite, presumably because the fuel line has not been sufficiently primed.  Ignition was sometimes unsuccessful because the settings for the automatic flame detection are such that detection threshold is reached because of the igniter glow rather than a flame.  As a result of the detection, the hot-wire igniter is deactivated and retracted, which is of course an issue if the flame has yet to ignite. This is typically avoided by detecting ignition with measurement of the flame’s OH* chemiluminescence with a Photomultiplier Tube (PMT) module.  The OH* chemiluminescence, in the ultraviolet at 310 nm, is a good indicator of an ignited flame rather than the glowing igniter, which emits primarily in the infrared and visible spectrum.  However, the combination of igniter settings and PMT gains can lead to false ignition detection.

**C. Completeness/Quality of Data**

The number of flames ignited significantly exceeds the planned tests which were (1) specified as required in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD), using the gas-jet burner, and (2) later expanded to include tests with the coflow burner to partially make up for science loss resulting from the slow response time of the highvoltage power supply. In contrast, 219 flames were ignited in the experiment, so nearly three times as many flames were ignited than required.  
It should be understood that a complete set of image data is not available for all tests.  As discussed in section III.B, the IPSU-1 was not working at the beginning of the second round of testing, preventing use of both the HiBMs camera and the CIR’s collimated illumination package. Furthermore, recorded image data is sometimes deleted without downlinking.  This is done because of operational constraints which limit the amount of data that can be managed per test day. **III. Results**
**D. Status of Data Analysis**

Data from the tests making up the E-FIELD Flames experiment includes video recordings from the operations camera for general flame behavior, high resolution images from the ACME data camera at various exposures and frame rates as dictated by the flame luminosity, intensified camera images, and non-imaging data at 125 Hz.  The non-imaging data file is processed using Matlab scripts (modified from those developed by CLD Flame researchers) to separately show trends of ion current and flame luminosity as a function of the applied field, and the flame parameters (fuel, flowrate, burner type).  The PMT data is also extracted to evaluate flame luminosity oscillations.  Image data is processed using the OMA software (also developed and used by CLD Flame researchers).
**III. Results**
**D. Status of Data Analysis**

The overall data volume is large with a storage limit of 127,000 MB per test day.  All of the data has been downloaded to the hard drive with a backup system at UC Irvine.  At this stage, the data has been sorted into appropriate segments so that comparisons can be made between burner geometries (jet versus coflow from the prior round of testing), fuel type and dilution (methane versus ethylene; no dilution, modest dilution, high dilution) and fuel flow velocity.  The fuel flow velocity and dilution conditions were sometimes selected to hold total carbon flux into the flame constant.  At this stage, the analysis remains comparative and qualitative, to show the major differences in behavior in microgravity and normal-gravity (1-g) flames, and to show particularly how buoyancy modifies the electrical response of the flames.
**III. Results**
**E. Preliminary Research Findings**

Distinctly different results were seen in E-FIELD Flames’ second round tests with the gasjet burner when compared with the first round tests with the coflow burner.  For example, the ion current response to the electric field strength with an upward ion driven wind in microgravity is a clear parabolic trend (which is similar to the trend observed in 1-g flames with the coflow burner as presented in the prior report).  The parabolic behavior is evident even with the strong oscillations observed during the rise.  This rising trend is not observed with the coflow burner.
**III. Results**
**E. Preliminary Research Findings**

The behavior of the soot and its charge state are complicated since in the regions of high field strength, particularly near the fuel tube where the field lines converge, soot can emit or collect free charges.  Hence, the soot transport is driven directly by the field and by the ion-driven wind (and thermophoresis) which means it can travel differentially to the bulk flow.  These various transport elements can push the soot through the flame to burnout, hold it in stasis in the flame for additional growth, or drive it to the burner where it accumulates.  More work is needed to sort through these elements.

_The s-Flame investigation is one of several independent experiments that are part of the ACME project, which uses a single modular set of hardware to carry out studies of flames burning gaseous fuels in the ISS’ Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR).  The first round of s-Flame tests was conducted during Increments 60 and 61, while the second round was conducted fully within Increment 63.  There were no tests conducted in Increment 62 because of limited crew availability._

**I. Introduction**

Tests for the Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame) experiment were conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  The purpose of s-Flame is to advance the ability to predict the structure and dynamics, including extinction and instabilities, of both soot-free and sooty flames.  The results may contribute to the development of lean-burn engines for improved efficiency and reduced pollutant emissions here on Earth.
**I. Introduction**

The spherical flames are ignited at non-steady conditions and allowed to transition naturally towards steady-state or extinction.  Tests are conducted with various inert diluents in both the fuel and chamber (oxidizer) atmosphere.  The fuel gases include hydrogen and methane mixtures for soot-free flames, and ethylene for sooty flames.  One experimental objective is to identify the extinction limits for both radiative and chemical kinetic extinction, i.e., where the flame extinguishes from radiative heat loss or is “blown out,” respectively.  Another objective is to determine the existence, onset, and nature of pulsating instabilities that have been theoretically predicted to occur in flames with certain fuel/inert mixtures at near-limit conditions.

**I. Introduction**

ACME/s-Flame – 30-Day Operation Accomplishments Report for ISS Increment 63  
More specifically, s-Flame has the following experimental objectives:  
- A. Measure and characterize the transient structure (such as temperature and species distribution) of diffusion flames established at initially non-steady, spherical flame structures for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty), for different flow rates.  
- B. Determine the quasi-steady convective/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (low system Damköhler numbers) and radiative/chemical-kinetic extinction limits (high system Damköhler numbers) for mixtures of different H2/CH4/diluent ratios (soot-free) and different C2H4/diluent ratios (sooty).
**I. Introduction**

- A. Determine the existence (for different Zeldovich number, Ze), onset (as a function Da), and nature (i.e. mode, frequency, amplitude) of pulsating instabilities theoretically predicted to occur in transient spherical diffusion flames using fuel/diluent mixtures that are above a critical Lewis number, at near-limit conditions.  
As suggested by the experiment’s name, s-Flame features a spherically symmetric diffusion flame, which is generated by discharging a fuel gas from a porous spherical burner into a still oxygen/inert atmosphere in microgravity.  The one-dimensional nature of the system facilitates data acquisition, data reduction, and computational simulation.
**I. Introduction**

The space flight program consists of two main parts: (1) Mapping and characterization of the motion (e.g., expansion) of spherical diffusion flames subsequent to ignition and at extinction because of the finite-rate chemistry and radiative heat loss.  The study is focused on the thermal radiation, the adequacy of the detailed chemistry and transport submodels used in computational modeling, and the development of flame front instabilities that could modify the extinction boundaries.  (2) Studies of the response of characteristically sooty flames to ignition, the onset of soot in the expanding flames, the soot radiation, and the soot’s effects on the flame spread, extinction, and instability.
**I. Introduction**

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the natural flicker of flames, which is a buoyancydriven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity. Characteristic length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure.  Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion systems, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normal-gravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment. The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior
**I. Introduction**

many microgravity flames are soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important. For example, chemi-ion species, electronically-excited chemiluminescent species, are at very low concentration in typical flames, making the reduced buoyancy environment valuable for evaluating the minor species chemistry.  With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application.

**II. Methods/Research Operations**
**A. Discussion of Method/Protocol**

The s-Flame investigation and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew.  The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.  
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC).  The science portion of the tests were all conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  As expected, no s-Flame tests were conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.  Thus far, that has been the case for all ACME tests, with the mundane exception of ‘manually’ halting the test after the flame has extinguished or perhaps if a temperature has reached a critical value.
**II. Methods/Research Operations**
**A. Discussion of Method/Protocol**

Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.  
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.
**III. Results**
**A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight**

A total of 276 flames were ignited for the s-Flame experiment, with 29, 116, and 131 respectively ignited during Increments 60, 61, and 63.  These numbers neglect some flames which quenched promptly after ignition.  In this regard, science testing began at the end of Increment 60 and the first round of tests were completed during Increment 61.  No tests were conducted in Increment 62 due to a lack of crew time, where the second round of tests were fully conducted during Increment 63.  
The tests were conducted in two rounds, where the first was conducted in increments 60 and 61 featured 145 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen (i.e., in the chamber atmosphere) were diluted with nitrogen.  The second round conducted in increment 63 featured 131 flames (nominally) in which the fuel and oxygen were instead diluted with helium.

**III. Results**
**B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies**

Ignition of the flames presented a significant challenge to the experiment during this increment.  All of the flame tests were conducted where the fuel and chamber atmosphere were both diluted with helium rather than the nitrogen used in Increments 60 and 61.  The two gases’ properties are dramatically different making comparison testing very desirable for manifestation of different phenomena. Helium’s thermal conductivity is notably several times greater than that of nitrogen, so considerably more energy and power was required to ignite the flames.  The power level was slowly increased from test to test until ignition was finally achieved on the ninth test, where only seven flames were ignited of the 15 tests conducted on May 11 (20132), the first day for flames in Increment 63.  The cautious approach was taken because of concerns that the igniter tip might fail (i.e., burn out) if too much power was applied.  An igniter failure would have likely halted testing for weeks given the

After that first test day, the decision was made to have the igniter replaced with a coil rather than loop design which was believed to be more robust because of the thicker wire.  Furthermore, the igniter tip had not been replaced in months, and the tips do degrade with time, especially when they are not quickly retracted from the ignited flames.  The coil igniter was used successfully but still with caution, where flames were not always ignited successfully.  Subsequently, some tests were conducted in atmosphere with ~30% oxygen (by volume) instead of the planned ~21%.  As one would expect, that proved to be helpful for achieving ignition.   But the end result was that some tests were conducted with 21% oxygen, some at 30%, and some at both nominal concentrations.  Fortuitously, this mixture of conditions may provide deeper insight into the mechanisms of flame dynamics and response.

**III. Results**
**B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies**

The flow ranges of the selected Mass Flow Controllers (MFCs) was found to be a challenge, where it was discovered that the goal of studying both kinetic and radiative extinction was not always satisfactorily achieved because of flow rate constraints.  
At high flow rates, the burner does not produce spherically symmetric flames.  While nominally spherical at moderate flow rates, the flame’s center becomes increasing offset from the burner center.  More specifically, the flame is shifted toward the supply tube indicating that the sintered attachment of the porous sphere to the supply tube is more ‘open’ than the pores of the spherical burner.  In other words, the flow from the burner is not spherically symmetric.  At sufficiently high flow rates, the flame becomes obviously non-spherical, where it can appear to be ellipsoidal or even parabolic in shape.  In the latter case, the flame locally quenches near the supply tube.
**III. Results**
**B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies**

When at a small fraction of the maximum flow rate, Mass Flow Controller (MFC) performance has been seen to be poor during s-Flame testing, i.e., where actual flow rate differed from that desired.  However, this was not a surprise to those familiar with the hardware.  
Flow perturbations have been noticed in some s-Flame tests, where ACME’s MFCs used to control the flow of fuel, nitrogen, and oxidizer have unfortunately not always performed satisfactorily.  In tests conducted using the 1-slpm fuel MFC (where the flow range is on a nitrogen basis), the flow has been seen to overshoot and undershoot when first opening. **B. List of Preflight, In-flight, Postflight Anomalies**

As mentioned previously, s-Flame tests have sometimes automatically aborted (because of the controlling software script), where that is normally prior to gas flow and the activation of the igniter – which is typical for other ACME experiments.  As a result, there was little lost other than the available experimental time in the failed test attempt.  ACME aborts normally occur because of communication issues with an IPSU, which for example happened for tests 19304A5, 19352D3, 19352P1, 20024N1, and 20024J1.   A few other tests aborted because flow rates were accidentally specified outside of the range of the installed mass flow controller(s), where that included for example 19352A1, 19352D2, and 20013C2.  ACME aborts are infrequent, but there are sometimes days when they occur repeatedly as can be seen here.
**III. Results**
**C. Completeness/Quality of Data**

During Increments 60 and 61, nine days of tests were conducted during which 145 flames were ignited for the first round of testing.  In contrast, only 29 tests were specified as required or highly desired in the ACME Integrated Science Requirements Document (ISRD) for that round.  Therefore, a wealth of data was obtained for this round of testing which featured gaseous fuels diluted by nitrogen.
**III. Results**
**C. Completeness/Quality of Data**

However, there was a significant loss of data.  Most importantly, the first fuel bottle appeared to leak on installation (in Increment 60) and later on-orbit testing (in Increment 61) with other hydrogen/methane blends suggests that its fuel mixture would have been ideal for achieving science success.  Furthermore, there was significant image data loss on two different test days, specifically Sept. 13 (19256) and Dec. 18 (19352).  As a result, those test days were nominally repeated on Jan. 29 (20029) and Jan. 24 (20024), respectively (i.e., in a reversed order).  For these reasons, a simple comparison of the total number of flames ignited (145) with that specified as required or highly desired (29) for the first round of testing is somewhat misleading.

Computational simulations with detailed chemistry and transport of the test cases are underway.  Time-dependent simulations will be compared with the time-dependent experimental data, where tracking of the flamefront location is based on chemiluminescent emission.  Steady-state simulations will produce the Isola curves mapping flame response versus system Damkhöler number for given fuel mixtures.  The experimental cases will then be pin-pointed on the computational mappings to assess whether the experimental conditions are in quasi-steady state or near extinction limits, either kinetic or radiative.  Oscillation behavior will be correlated to possible pulsating oscillations found in the simulations.

To assess whether these nitrogen-diluted ethylene flames are non-sooty or sooty, cases were run where mixtures were ignited and established at low flow rates (e.g., 3 cc/s) with low ethylene contents (e.g., 25-30% C2H4) and then ramped to high flow rates (e.g., 5-10 cc/s) with higher ethylene contents (e.g., 40-50% C2H4).  The flames all radiatively extinguished, but no sooting was observed.  Observations of such radiative extinction behavior at high flow rates is an achievement because such phenomenon was not observed in our groundbased studies, given the limited microgravity durations. The 19256 tests (in Increment 60) were aimed at examining kinetic extinction.  Similar to the radiative extinction cases, sufficient microgravity duration is needed to observe kinetic extinction because a near steady flame needs to be established first, before ramp down in flow rate to find properly the chemical kinetic extinction limit.  High flow rate cases (e.g., 13.5 cc/s, 15 cc/s) showed asymmetrical flames which radiatively extinguished.  Flow rates were lowered so that quasi-steady flames could be established before ramp down in flow rate.  The 15% C2H4 mixtures were not strong enough to sustain a quasi-steady flame at 3 cc/s before ramp down.  However, for stronger mixtures, i.e., 20-30% C2H4, very nice flames were established at 3 cc/s; and kinetic extinctions were observed during ramp down before reaching 1 cc/s. **1.  Overview**

The CFI experiments are conceived as follow-up experiments to the FLEX and FLEX-2 droplet combustion experiments onboard the ISS to further explore the newly discovered quasi-steady “cool flames.”  Cool flames are controlled by low temperature chemistry, and occur in the NTC region of n-alkane fuels.  FLEX series of experiments showed for the first time that quasi-steady stable flames can be established surrounding a droplet in microgravity under certain conditions, without a visible flame at temperatures in the range of 700 to 900 K, unlike the hot flames where the flame temperature is higher than 1200 K.  Since the cool-flame chemistry depends on the chemical structure of the fuel as well as pressure and temperature, three different fuel combinations were investigated, namely, pure n-dodecane, n-dodecane/isododecane mixtures and farnesane ( a renewable jet fuel) at ambient pressures up to 5 atmospheres. Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental importance. With the emergence of newer internal combustion engine technologies such as Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) and Reactivity-Controlled Compression Ignition (RCCI) engines, understanding the autoignition and heat release chemistry and kinetics of hydrocarbon fuels is more important that ever. a. Objectives

Cool flame phenomena are influenced by a number of factors, including the fuel molecular structure (for pure fuel cases), the ambient environment (pressure, temperature, oxygen and diluent (He) concentrations), and the fuel composition (the mixture of fuel structures and perhaps fuel additives such as those used to change octane or cetane behavior). Though it is not possible to examine all of these factors in a thorough manner, here we propose a set of experiments that explore each one of these factors, namely, fuel structure effects, ambient conditions effect, fuel mixture effects, and the presence of fuel additives.

**3.  Science Overview**

- a. Background  
Understanding the combustion characteristics of liquid hydrocarbon fuels is of practical and fundamental importance. The United States alone consumes approximately 19 million barrels of liquid fuels per day, which averages out to an amazing 2.5 gallons per day per person.  The primary reason for such high reliance on hydrocarbon fuels as the single most important energy source, not only in the US but in the rest of the world, is their high energy density, ease of handling, and portability, compared to many other forms of energy sources. With the emergence of newer technologies for internal combustion engines and the increasing use of renewable bio-fuels, such as the Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition (HCCI) engine and bio-diesel, that promise cleaner more efficient and sustainable utilization of hydrocarbon fuels, the need to understand the fundamental chemical and physical aspects of liquid-fuel combustion is bound to increase.
**3.  Science Overview**

Commercially available transportation fuels, such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel, are comprised of many hydrocarbon compounds, normal alkanes and branched alkanes being major components. The combustion characteristics of these alkanes are quite complex and follow branched-chain reaction pathways involving many intermediate radicals. The chemical pathways vary, depending on temperature and, to a lesser extent, on pressure.  In general it is possible to identify a low-temperature reaction mechanism and a hightemperature mechanism, with a transition region between them. Many hydrocarbons exhibit a unique feature in this transition region, namely that the reaction rate decreases with increasing temperature,  
3  
leading it to be called the negative-temperature-coefficient (NTC) region. There area a number of models available in the literature, simplified chemical-kinetic model involving hundreds of reactions as well as detailed mechanisms involving thousands of reactions.
**3.  Science Overview**

Droplet-combustion experiments (FLEX, FLEX-2) conducted onboard the International Space Station, as part of the Flame Extinguishment Experiments, have revealed for the first time that large n-alkane droplets can continue to burn quasi-steadily in the NTC region (see, Fig 1). NTC behavior of the heat-release rate is necessary for low-temperature quasi-steady droplet burning to be stable. It was observed that the secondstage combustion of the droplet controlled by low-temperature NTC chemistry, referred to as ``cool-flame combustion" here for the sake of simplicity, abruptly ends at a finite droplet diameter, leaving the unburned droplet to vaporize in the hot atmosphere. A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the partially oxidized fuel condensed immediately following cool-flame extinction. 45 16

**3.  Science Overview**

Furthermore, the second-stage flame is shown to lie closer to the droplet surface where the rates of heat generation by the NTC chemistry is dynamically balanced by the heat loss rate. Unlike the hot-flame combustion where the overall process is controlled by equilibrium thermodynamic properties of the fuel, the cool-flame combustion depends on the chemical-kinetic details of the NTC region.  These experimental and numerical studies provide a new tool to further explore the NTC chemistry of liquid fuels in an entirely new way.  The experimental cool-flame droplet burning rates provide measures of the heat-release rates and stoichiometry, the flame-diameter evolution provides insight into hot-flame diffusive and convective heat-loss effects, and the droplet extinction diameter provides a stringent measurement of chemical-kinetic characteristic times.
**3.  Science Overview**

The objectives of the CFI experiments is to further explore the cool flame phenomenon using pure fuels, and fuel mixtures over a range of pressures and helium dilution.  
b. Rational for Microgravity (if unusual)  
4  
Rationale for microgravity remains the same for all the droplet combustion experiments conducted onboard the ISS. In microgravity the droplets burn in a spherically symmetric form, and therefore it is possible to model the processes with complex chemical kinetic mechanisms involving thousands of reactions leading to a better understanding of the chemistry.  Moreover, the cool flames need much longer residence times and cannot be observed under normal gravity conditions with droplet flames.

**4.  Operations**

- a. Procedures  
The operational procedure used in the CFI tests is the same as for the FLEX experiments. Once the ISS crew installs the required fuel syringe, and the gas bottles containing the gas mixtures in the MDCA and CIR facilities, all the actual experimental operations are conducted from the ground at the Telescience Support Center (TSC) located at the NASA Glenn Research Center.  Prior to each test the combustion chamber is filled with the specified gas mixture at the required pressure, and the hot-wire igniters are positioned close to the droplet deployment site.  Subsequently, a droplet of desired size is dispensed between the hypodermic needles and freely deployed, and ignited.  The igniter is withdrawn from the FOV once ignition is detected. When required a 40 micron silicon-carbide fiber is used to tether the droplet at one place and stop it from drifting off from the field of view.
**4.  Operations**

The combustion process is recorded using a backlit, black-and-white camera ( 5 cm X 5 cm FOV) to obtain droplet size as a function of time, a UV-sensitive camera is used to image the OH* emission from the flame which provides the flame size data.  A color camera which is had a live downlink to the TSC is used to perform and monitor the overall process.  Narrow-band and wide-band radiometers are used to measure the radiation emission from the flame.  Details of the experimental hardware and the data reduction procedures can be found in Dietrich et al. (2014)  
- b. On-Orbit Testing  
Over two hundred tests were carried out during the CFI experimental campaign.  The initial droplet size was kept around 4 mm so that radiative extinction and the subsequent cool flame combustion can be observed. The list of experiments performed are as follows:  
- Pure n-dodecane at 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 2, 3, and 5 atm.
**4.  Operations**

- Pure n-dodecane at 0.5, 0.75, 1, 1.25, 2, 3, and 5 atm.  
- N-dodecane/Iso-dodecane mixtures: 75/25% and 60/40% by mass at pressures from 0.5 to 5 atm  
- Helium dilution by 29% and 59% with O2 mole fraction at 0.21  
- Farnesane: from 0.75 to 3 atm  
- c. Anomalies That Effect Science Surprises/New Discovery  
No new anomalies or surprises were observed during the CFI experiments. However, as the ambient pressure is increased above 2 atm, multiple reignition cycles were observed, where first the hot flame extinguishes due to radiative heat loss followed by cool flame, and then reignition to a hot-flame followed by a cool flame, with this cycle repeating several times until the fuel droplet is completely consumed. This behavior is unexpected based on earlier observations from FLEX experiments. Furthermore, the soot-shell

5.4 _<u>Sooting behavior as function of ambient pressure:</u>_

The effects and the process of soot formation during cool flame combustion remains largely unexplored. The shoot shell that forms during hot flame is stabilized by the balance of force between fluid mechanical drag and the thermophoretic force. At low pressures a stable spherical soot-shell is formed. However, as the pressure increase the soot-shell becomes diffuse and undefined.  The reasons for this phenomenon is still not well understood. At low pressures, due to the low flame temperature of the cool flame, soot is not formed. The soot that is formed during the hot flame combustion is simply convected away from the droplet surface. But, when the pressure increases, residual soot is seen surrounding the droplet even after the hot flame extinction.  The mechanisms behind this process has not been fully understood, and further analysis and research is needed.

5.5 Summary of findings:

CFI experiments has provided cool flame burning data for pure n-dodecane, and n-dodecane/iso-dodecane mixtures.  Farnesane, a commercially available renewable fuel characteristics were also studied.  The effect of pressure and helium dilution were studied for these fuels. Data for droplet regression rate, hot and cool flame diameters, extinction conditions, and radiant emission, both broad band and narrow band, are obtained and posted to the PSI website.
b. Benefits

Low temperature chemistry is of fundamental importance in the combustion of many practical fuels.  Low temperature chemistry controls the autoignition of fuels when injected into a combustion chamber, and in homogeneous mixtures of fuel and oxygen.  New internal combustion engines, such as the HCCI engines, operate at low temperatures reducing the pollution formation and increasing overall efficiencies. The CFI experimental measurements provide a useful way to validate the complex chemical kinetic mechanisms that are being developed. The cool flame combustion process itself maybe of use in fuel reformulation technologies to produce hydrogen in fuel cell applications.

##### **Abstract**
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

Leaks, fires, and spills are some of the most significant hazards that must be accounted for in the design of the environmental control and life-support system on spacecraft. While prevention is certainly the first line of defense against a fire, early detection of a overheat event or an actual fire allows the crew to respond before the hazard gets out of control. The limited options available for response to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications. The SAME experiments were conducted during Expedition 15 on the ISS. **1. Introduction**

Appropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters.  Terrestrial fire detection systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.<sup>1, 2</sup> Unfortunately, there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently current spacecraft fire detectors were developed based upon experience on normal gravity fire behavior and properties. This approach was necessary given the absence of data concerning microgravity smoke particulate. However planned spacecraft and their planned missions outside of low earth-orbit will require increased reliability of fire detection systems in addition to robust false alarm resistance.  Extended lunar-surface missions will require systems that are not influenced by lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources.

**1. Introduction**

The absence of buoyant flow increases the residence time in microgravity fires causing substantial changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire behavior seen in reduced gravity, it is reasonable to expect that the signatures and detection requirements of these fires will change. There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.<sup>3</sup> The materials used in spacecraft are different from those typically used in terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. More importantly, the limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications. **2. Smoke Background**

Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes.  In particular for non-flaming combustion, the aerosol includes recondensed original material or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid.  For flaming combustion, the aerosol includes soot particulate, condensed water vapor, and ash particles.  Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth.  Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.

**3. SAME Experiment**

To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) was developed.  The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth. A. <u>The Moment Method</u>

The approach used by the SAME experiment is termed the ‘moment method’ for convenience.<sup>13</sup> This approach consists of measuring three moments of the size distribution (the zeroth, first and third moment) on orbit, using several small, light-weight instruments.  By applying the properties of the lognormal distribution to the measured moments, the total number concentration, _Nt_ , the geometric mean diameter, _Dg_ , and the geometric standard deviation,  _g_ , of the aerosol can be estimated. Once these three parameters are known, the size distribution of the measured aerosol is uniquely defined, assuming that the distribution is lognormal. In what follows, we will explain how the moment method works.

A.2. Implementation of the moment method in SAME experiment

In the SAME experiment, the zeroth moment, _M0_ , was measured using a condensation nuclei counter called the P-Trak<sup>TM</sup> (TSI Inc.). The first moment, _M1_ , was approximately proportional to the output signal of an ionization detector, which was a modified ionization chamber taken from a commerciallyavailable smoke detector. The third moment, _M3_ , was inferred from the light scattered by the smoke aerosol when illuminated by a red laser. For particles in the size range of 0.2 μm to 2.0 μm, , the light scattering signal at 90 degrees from a red laser is approximately proportional to the third moment. The instrument used to obtain the third moment is called a DustTrak<sup>TM</sup> (TSI Inc.). Calibration measurements were made for the DustTrak to account for the departure of the scattering signal from the 3<sup>rd</sup> moment. B. <u>Instrumentation</u>  
The moment measurements were made using an assembly of three separate instruments. Two are industrial hygiene instruments manufactured by TSI and one is a modified residential smoke detector.
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
A.3. Uncertainty Analysis

The zeroth-moment instrument is a condensation nuclei counter, the P-Trak™ (TSI Inc.).  This device operates by passing the aerosol-laden air stream through a region saturated with isopropanol vapor and then into a cooler region where the vapor condenses onto the particles increasing their diameter such that they can be readily counted by a light scattering device.  This instrument is very robust and operates over a range of 0 to 10<sup>5</sup> particles/cm<sup>3</sup> and 20 nm to 1 μm diameter.  Some dilution is required since the smoke concentration in SAME ranges from about 0.5 × 10<sup>6</sup> to 5 × 10<sup>6</sup> particles/cm<sup>3</sup> . There was also a concern that the isopropanol condensate would not return to the wick in low-gravity.<sup>5</sup> To mitigate this  
9
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)
A.3. Uncertainty Analysis

9  
issue, the condensing section of the device was modified with very small grooves to improve conductance of the condensate back to the wick.  These changes were tested in a separate space experiment with good results indicating the modified device could be used successfully in low gravity.<sup>5</sup>  
The first-moment instrument is the ionization chamber taken from a residential smoke detector. This device uses an alpha-particle emitter to generate ions in a region within a DC electric field. Normally, the ions drift toward an electrode inside the ionization chamber producing a current.  When particulate are present, the ions attach themselves to the particles thereby charging the particles. Because the charged particles have a much smaller mobility than ions alone, the current is reduced. The required particle concentrations are on the order of 10<sup>5</sup> particles/cm<sup>3</sup> , thus no sample dilution was required.
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

The third-moment instrument is a light scattering device, the DustTrak™ (TSI Inc.).  The device uses a 90 degree light scattering signal to quantify the aerosol mass density.  For terrestrial dust particulate, this signal correlates well with the mass concentration, however additional compensation was needed to account for the range of particle sizes observed in the SAME experiment.  The device operating range is from 0.001 mg/m<sup>3</sup> to 100 mg /m<sup>3</sup> .  These devices are equipped with an aerodynamic impactor at the inlet which captures particles larger than the selected size.  The SAME experiment included 2 DustTraks™, one with a 1 μm impactor and the other with a 10 μm impactor.  The difference in the signal from the two devices provided a measure of the fraction of the particulate that was larger than 1 μm.  In some cases dilution was required owing to the high smoke concentration levels.

Calibration of these instruments was essential to properly interpret the flight data and was performed on the ground before the flight. Realizing that crew time was the most precious ISS resource, SAME was designed to be operated both autonomously and from the ground to the greatest extent possible. The SAME hardware was organized into a number of smaller modular units to facilitate stowage for launch, provide for easy change out, increase the reliability and reduce risk. The downside of this strategy was that the assembly of the experiment involved many connections and required approximately 5 hours of crew time. Once installed, however, SAME was easily and effectively operated from the Tele Science Center (TSC) at the Glenn Research Center (GRC), and this capability enabled the ground team to achieve roughly a 50% greater number of test points (and data) than was originally planned.

**4. Flight Tests**

The on orbit operations were scheduled around the availability of the crew for installing the next Sample Carousel and Thermal Precipitator (and removing and stowing the used ones). Typically, the crew would install the next units during the morning, and operations would be scheduled for later that day. SAME would be nominally scheduled by the ISS staff for two test points on each of the following days.  
14  
Because the allowed operations windows were sufficiently large, the ground team was frequently able to perform four test points in the allowed time.  
The staffing level of the ground team varied between two and five members from the engineering team with additional support from up to three members of the Science team. Most of the time, there would be one person operating the linked computer that controlled the experiment, one providing verbal communication to the ISS cadre and doing data reduction and a third recording video and performing other miscellaneous functions.

Uplink parameter sheets were generated by the Science team and most times, emailed to the engineering team the day before operations, although when additional unplanned test points were performed during a session, the Science team provided a hard copy of the parameters during the interim between test points. These sheets were printed and checked, and in most cases, signed. The parameters were entered into the ground computer by a team member and then the entry was checked both by means of a checksum and by the other member on consol before uplinking them to the DACU.

**4. Flight Tests**

The test points were scheduled by the ground team to coincide with Ku and S band coverage so that video of the heating and the measurement data could be obtained Near Real Time (NRT) and recorded on the ground. Because the data reduction software was already in place, processing of the data could be done immediately after the test point had been completed, and in all cases, before the next test point was performed. Periodically during the overall operations, downloads from the DACU were commanded as a backup to the NRT data to insure that the most complete compilation was available.

Based on the results of an earlier flight project carried out in the Glovebox of the Space Shuttle, (Comparative Soot Diagnostics (CSD)), the soot particles generated and observed in low gravity environment tend to be larger in size than those in earth conditions. However, the preliminary results of CSD project were not conclusive because of a minor variation of the temperature of hot wire which heated the test sample to generate smoke, and also because the CSD apparatus could not measure the liquid drops existing in the smoke produced by several of the samples. Furthermore, the CSD project was not designed to provide on-orbit measurement of the particle size distribution. The Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment was designed to obtain this data that could then be used to design the next-generation smoke detectors for space exploration missions. Unfortunately, because of the relatively small volume of the MSG, it cannot accommodate the instruments normally used in a ground-based
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

missions. Unfortunately, because of the relatively small volume of the MSG, it cannot accommodate the instruments normally used in a ground-based laboratory to measure the size distribution of smoke particulate. Therefore, a new procedure was developed, the moment method, from which the characteristics of the particle size distribution can be inferred using a minimum number of portable instrument.
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

The SAME experiments were conducted during Expedition 15 on the ISS.  Four materials, typical of those found in spacecraft, were tested including cellulose (lamp wick), Kapton, silicone rubber, and Teflon. A fifth material, dibutyl-phthalate (DBP) retained in a cotton wick was used as a reference. In order to simulate the detection of a pre-fire overheated-material event, samples were heated to temperatures below the ignition point. The smoke generation conditions were controlled to provide repeatable sample surface temperatures and air flow conditions. The transport time from the smoke source to the detector was simulated by holding the smoke in an aging chamber for times ranging from 10 seconds to 1800 seconds.  Smoke particle samples were collected on Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) grids for post-flight analysis. The smoke properties were measured using particulate aerosol diagnostics that measure different moments of the size distribution. These statistics were combined to
Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME)

were measured using particulate aerosol diagnostics that measure different moments of the size distribution. These statistics were combined to determine the geometric mean particle sizes and geometric standard deviation, which is sufficient to describe the entire smoke distribution if a lognormal distribution is assumed. the ISS and the space shuttle were also included in the SAME apparatus. The experimental results show that, for the materials tested, a substantial portion of the smoke particles are below 500 nm in diameter. The smoke transport model demonstrated that mixing dominates the smoke transport and that consequently detection time lags are longer than in normal gravity. The knowledge gained from SAME can be used to establish design requirements for smoke detectors used in future spacecraft.

**1. Introduction**

Appropriate design of fire detection systems requires knowledge of both the expected signature of the events to be detected and the background levels of the measured parameters.  Terrestrial fire detection systems have been developed based on extensive study of terrestrial fires.<sup>1, 2</sup> Unfortunately, there is no corresponding data set for spacecraft fires and consequently current spacecraft fire detectors were developed based upon experience on normal gravity fire behavior and properties. This approach was necessary given the absence of data concerning microgravity smoke particulate. However planned spacecraft and their planned missions outside of low earth-orbit will require increased reliability of fire detection systems in addition to robust false alarm resistance.  Extended lunar-surface missions will require systems that are not influenced by lunar dust and other nuisance dust sources.

**1. Introduction**

The absence of buoyant flow increases the residence time in microgravity fires causing substantial changes in flame structure. Given the large changes in fire behavior seen in reduced gravity, it is reasonable to expect that the signatures and detection requirements of these fires will change. There are a number of factors that can be expected to affect the particle size distribution of the smoke from spacecraft fires. The absence of buoyant flow in low-gravity increases the residence time in microgravity fires and increases the transit time from the reaction zone to the detector.<sup>3</sup> The materials used in spacecraft are different from those typically used in terrestrial applications where smoke properties were previously evaluated. More importantly, the limited options available to respond to a spacecraft fire increase the importance of detecting the fire in an earlier stage of its development than is typical for terrestrial applications.  All of these effects can be expected

**2. Smoke Background**

Smoke is a general term that encompasses aerosol materials produced by a number of processes.  In particular for non-flaming combustion, the aerosol includes recondensed original material or pyrolysis products that can be either liquid or solid.  For flaming combustion, the aerosol includes soot particulate, condensed water vapor, and ash particles.  Soot particles dominate the smoke particulate in established flaming fires while unburned pyrolysis products and recondensed polymer fragments are produced by smoldering and pyrolysis in the early stage of fire growth.  Given the constrained space on any spacecraft, the target for the fire detection system is necessarily the early phase and not established flaming fires; consequently, the primary target for detection is the pyrolysis products and not the soot.

**3. SAME Experiment**

To address the limited data from the CSD experiment concerning the likely size of spacecraft smoke particulate, the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) was developed.  The SAME experiment sought to avoid the problems experienced by the CSD experiment by obtaining the particulate size statistics on-orbit with a reduced dependence upon sample return to Earth.  This is a challenging endeavor because existing aerosol instrumentation is typically too large to be compatible with spacecraft experiment constraints. Thus, to obtain particulate size statistics with existing aerosol instrumentation would require the return of numerous samples to Earth.  As will be described below, an alternative approach was employed that used three discrete instruments to measure separate moments of the size distribution.  When combined, these moments provide useful aggregate statistics of the size distribution if a lognormal distribution is assumed.  The measurements were made using smoke generated by

A. <u>The Moment Method</u>

The approach used by the SAME experiment is termed the ‘moment method’ for convenience.<sup>13</sup> This approach consists of measuring three moments of the size distribution (the zeroth, first and third moment) on orbit, using several small, light-weight instruments.  By applying the properties of the lognormal distribution to the measured moments, the total number concentration, _Nt_ , the geometric mean diameter, _Dg_ , and the geometric standard deviation,  _g_ , of the aerosol can be estimated. Once these three parameters are known, the size distribution of the measured aerosol is uniquely defined, assuming that the distribution is lognormal. In what follows, we will explain how the moment method works.

A.1. Principle of the moment method

If _fN(D)_ is an arbitrary function, all its moments are independent of each other making it impossible to reconstruct _fN(D)_ from a finite number of its moments. Thus, this type of distribution function, _fN(D)_ , can always be constructed if the independent moments are known. This is the underlying idea of the moment method.
