A reexamination of updated transport parameters for the LLNL model is thus suggested.

Observations of long-duration cool flame burning of isolated _n_ -alkane droplets with a large initial diameter (Do) under microgravity conditions [1-5] demonstrate an interesting venue for the study of diffusive cool flame burning. In counterflow, pre-vaporized, laminar diffusion flame configurations, the addition of ozone to the oxidizer flow stream has been demonstrated as a mean of achieving stabilized cool flame burning conditions [12-14]. The simulations are performed using numerically-reduced kinetic models for _n_ - C7H16 [19] and _n_ -C10H22 [20] combustion developed previously. The _n_ -C7H16 and _n_ -C10H22 models consist of 128 species undergoing 565 elementary reactions and 233 species undergoing 1266 elementary reactions respectively. The coupled set of partial differential and algebraic equations are discretized in two steps- first in space and then integrated temporally as a set of coupled ordinary differentialalgebraic equations. A node-centered finite volume approach with 2<sup>nd</sup> order accuracy is employed for spatial discretization. The interface between the gas and liquid phases outlines the volume boundaries. The inner zone corresponds to the liquid phase fuel while the outer zone represents the gas phase ambient including the far-field which is defined as two hundred times the initial droplet diameter. Prescribed fixed ambient composition and temperature are constrained in the far-field as typical Dirichlet boundary conditions. The innermost liquid node serves as the center of origin imposing the no-flux condition. In order to avoid oscillatory solutions, the discretized mass flux is calculated on the cell faces instead of cell centers. The final set of discretized equations are then numerically

The potential for direct initiation of cool flame burning for a sub-millimeter size _n_ - C7H16 droplet with O3 addition is first explored conceptually by employing two different initiation energy deposition approaches. In the first, the entire ambient temperature field is raised at time zero-from 298 K to 425 K (hot ambient approach). In summary, the combined effects of initiation energy, and ozone-stimulated chemical heat release from initially present fuel vapor oxidation play key roles in establishing a sustained cool flame droplet burning behaviors for sub-millimeter sized low flash point fuels such as _n_ -C7H16.  While hot flame droplet burning can always be established, appropriate seeding levels of ozone and lower initiation energies can result in establishing direct cool flame droplet burning, even for fuels with flash points below droplet and ambient initial temperatures.  However, in all cases, heat release from the

stimulated reaction of initially vaporized fuel near the drop surface will limit and may even preclude the ability to establish cool flame burning behavior. The next section compares the establishment of low temperature burning characteristics of fuels that have significantly different thermophysical properties.

Recent experiments with large diameter _n_ -decane ( _n_ -C10H22) droplets on board the ISS demonstrated that for fuels and conditions where ambient temperatures are below the flash point, the _overall_ ignition characteristics are significantly more dependent on the thermal initiation energy that is applied. For these fuels, the liquid surface temperature must be raised above the flashpoint in order to supply flammable vapor/air mixtures near the drop, and initially, there is very little vapor/air mixtures for reactions to be stimulated by ozone seeding. As a result, the initiation energy deposition characteristics control the initial rate of flammable vapor development surrounding the drop, thus offering control of the ozone seeded chemical heat release properties that can contribute to thermally driving the vapor phase autoignition and transition to vapor phase droplet burning. **6.5 CONCLUDING REMARKS**

Isolated _n_ -alkane ( _n_ -C7H16 and _n_ -C10H22) droplet combustion was computationally investigated for different initial diameters (Do = 0.1, 0.5 mm), ambient pressures (1, 25 atm) with selected levels of O3 in the surrounding. The prime objective of this study was to explore whether cool flame droplet burning can be directly established for submillimeter sized _n_ -alkane droplets at conditions where radiative extinction is unlikely. Computations were performed for _n_ -C7H16 and _n_ -C10H22 fuels, as low and high flash point exemplars. Summarizing the results of this analysis:  
1. The required initiation energy for igniting low and high flashpoint (relative to ambient temperature) fuel droplets differ as a result of combustion of partially premixed flammable vapor present in the low flashpoint case. The rapid combustion of this

**7.1 ABSTRACT**

This chapter reports simulation results of oscillatory cool flame burning of an isolated, sub-millimeter sized n-heptane (n-C7H16) droplet in a selectively ozone seeded nitrogen-oxygen environments at atmospheric pressure. An evolutionary one-dimensional droplet combustion code, as discussed at length in chapter 2, encompassing relevant physics and detailed chemistry was employed to explore the roles of low-temperature chemistry, ozone seeding, and dynamic flame structure on burning behaviors. For XO2=21% and a range of selective ozone seeding,  near-quasi-steady cool flame burning is achieved directly (without requiring hot flame initiation and radiative extinction). Under low oxygen index conditions, with 5% ozone seeding (v/v), a nearly quasi-steady cool flame is initially established that then transitions to a dynamically oscillating cool flame burning mode until the droplet is completely consumed. It is found that the oscillation is initiated by the depletion of fuel

In this chapter, we numerically investigate the oscillatory cool flame behavior of O3 assisted sub-millimeter sized (Do=0.5 mm) n-C7H16 droplet burning at atmospheric conditions (P=1 atm, T=298 K) and two reduced oxygen indices (XO2 = 10% and 15%) that bracket the known limiting oxygen index (LOI)  (about 13%) for spherosymmetric n- heptane droplet combustion [24]. To assess the influence of ozone in the pulsing behavior, simulations were conducted for a range of ozone loadings. The temporal evolution of Tmax for these cases is summarized in Figure 7.7. It is clear that the ozone content of the ambient strongly influences the oscillation patterns. For an oxygen index that is lower than the LOI, the pulsing magnitude decreases with increasing ozone loading. In addition, the pulse frequency is also found to increase as the ozone fraction is increased. For a critical ozone level of XO3 = 6.0%, the system transitions to hot-flame burning. It can be inferred from the analysis that under near limit conditions (i.e. LOI) the ozone which was introduced to permit direct initiation of cool flame burning also perturbs the cool flame burning behavior. However, this perturbation effect diminishes and becomes small when larger oxygen index conditions are applied.

**7.5 CONCLUDING REMARKS**

The dynamics of near-limit cool flame burning of isolated sub-millimeter sized n-  
heptane (n-C7H16) droplet (Do = 0.5 mm) has been numerically investigated under atmospheric pressure condition. To provide the necessary near limit constraint, the oxygen in the ambient was set to a value that is lower than the limiting oxygen index (LOI) criteria for n-C7H16 and ozone (O3) was seeded (5% v/v) to the ambient to accomplish cool flame initiation. Based on the detailed analysis, the following features can be drawn as highlighting points for this computational study.  
1. At an atmospheric O2 concentration (21%) with 5% O3 (both v/v), sub-millimeter sized n-C7H16 droplet attains direct initiation of cool flame upon ignition energy initialization. Heat feedback to the droplet surface stemming from the consequence of ‘pre-vaporized fuel + atomic O’ reaction contributes as secondary initiation energy.
**Combustion Behavior Of Sub-Millimeter Sized Oxygenated And N- Alkane Fuel Droplets**
**OSCILLATORY COOL FLAME BEHAVIOR OF SUBMILLIMETER SIZED N-ALKANE DROPLET UNDER NEAR LIMIT CONDITIONS**
**7.5 CONCLUDING REMARKS**

2. For the exemplary reduced O2 case (10%), the resultant ignition energy escalates the local gas phase temperature ~1150 K, consuming the fuel vapor near the droplet, and

simultaneously increasing the O2 mole fraction ~16% (v/v) following the decomposition of O3. Due to the diffusive/thermo-kinetic balance of heat generation, the system attains a quasi-steady cool flame burn for a brief period of time which then enters an ever-oscillatory low-temperature cool flame burn.  
3. It is found that within each full oscillatory cycle, the maximum local gas phase temperature (i.e., flame) resides closest to the droplet, and the flame positions itself to the furthest radial location when its value reaches the cycle minima. At each successive pulse, the flame region (including the reaction zone) progressively grows outward as a result of continuous fuel leakage through the flame location.

Further analyses indicate that the dynamic interaction of degenerate chain branching and chain termination/propagation reaction classes of QOOH associated with the low temperature and NTC kinetic regimes, and continuous fuel leakage across the flame location contribute to the ever-increasing trends of the oscillation magnitude. It is found that while the progression of QOOH  chain propagation/termination reaction class directly correlates with the gas phase temperature field within a full oscillation cycle, the QOOH  degenerate branching reactions undergo three distinct stages within the same oscillation cycle. The oscillatory burning, which essentially is a perturbation effect resulting from the presence of ozone, is prominent under low ozone loading and diminishes as the ozone fraction in the system is increased.

**8.1 PREFACE TO CLOSURE**

Combustion of sub-millimeter sized (Do < 1.0 mm) isolated sphero-symmetric liquid fuel droplets has been numerically studied in this thesis work employing onedimensional CFD code for renewable alcohol fuels and higher n-alkanes. Methanol (CH3OH) and butanol (C4H9OH, including its four isomers) represent the first category of fuels while n-heptane (n-C7H16) and n-decane (n-C10H22) consist of the second category. Two major forms of flame configurations, namely high temperature and low temperature (including cool) flames, have been extensively studied. In this dissertation, results pertaining to the high-temperature flames are exclusively related to the renewable alcohol fuels, while the low-temperature flames are examined through the higher n-alkanes. To emulate the practical droplet combustion in reduced or near-absence of gravity condition, all the relevant physics are incorporated in the modeling formulation along with detailed description of kinetics. For selective case studies,

The strength of the current version of isolated droplet combustion CFD code stems from the simplicity of low dimensional flow field that augments the coupling of large kinetics and other associated thermo-fluid sub-models.  To further transcend its capability, the following recommendations are provided in light of the experiences harnessed through the course of this dissertation work. The author believes that each of the three proposals reported here could be a Ph.D. and/or M.S. level research topic by their own prospect for future exploration.

- a. Sooting fuel simulation. To model the sooting fuels, currently, the CFD code has two versions of soot model, namely- the BIN method [1] and the moment method [2]. Both of these soot modeling methods are fairly detailed in nature, therefore the simulation complexity increases tremendously when coupled with detailed gas phase kinetics. A potential way forward to address the soot modeling for droplet combustion is to incorporate semi-detailed soot modeling [3] to reduce the simulation turn over time.

b. The inclusion of real gas formulation. The ideal gas law is a typically the default choice for the equation of states (EOS) for most of the available commercial and in-house legacy codes. This simplified formulation of EOS is found to work satisfactorily at ambient and above ambient pressures for both the reacting and nonreacting CFD simulations. However, ideal gas law starts to underperform significantly as the gas phase system approaches critical pressure regime for the species of interests. Therefore, to address this concern, the real gas effect should be included and the overall code structure has to be updated and validated against experimental targets accordingly.

Although the one-dimensional droplet combustion is simple in terms of fluid physics, it is relevant to the complex spray combustion by incorporating moving boundary effects, unsteady heat transfer, mass diffusion to and from the droplet surface, temperature dependent variable properties, phase equilibrium at the interface and radiative perturbation. In order to progress towards real spray arrangement without compromising in terms of kinetic aspect, the next step should be to include multi-dimensional effect for isolated droplet combustion. Project Overview

This research provides quantitative correlations between solidification and flow characteristics, processing conditions, microstructure, and porosity for solder joints produced in terrestrial vs. microgravity conditions (onboard the International Space Station (ISS)).  Furthermore, this project focuses on analyzing solder joint properties under extreme conditions of elevated and cryogenic temperatures in space. Soldering is the predominant method used to create electrical/mechanical joints and mechanical/pressure joints and is typically a rapid process in which the solder material is molten for only a few seconds. Solder joint porosity is a common but undesirable feature naturally arising from the use of fluxes and is more insidious in soldering joints formed under microgravity conditions. Under the presence of gravity, voids and bubbles are removed from the solder joints due to presence of buoyancy force and vigorous liquid solder mixing. In the _absence_ of gravity, fluid motion is

are removed from the solder joints due to presence of buoyancy force and vigorous liquid solder mixing. In the _absence_ of gravity, fluid motion is greatly reduced, driven mainly by solidification volume change, thermally induced density gradients, and Marangoni effects. With slower mixing, voids and bubbles are not swept away and become entrapped in the interior of the solder joint upon solidification.  This entrapped porosity dramatically degrades the thermal and electrical properties of the solder and severely reduces the mechanical integrity of the joint. Therefore, as part of the ongoing endeavors to establish an electronics and mechanical joint repair capability for extended space missions, this project seeks to advance the current understanding of fundamental mechanisms, phenomenology, and process conditions that govern the integrity and performance of solder joints produced in terrestrial vs. reduced gravity environments. Project Overview

This project focused on the following objectives to address the reliability of solder joints in space: 1) Characterizing the effects of the lack of Earth's natural convective flow and buoyancy on solderjoint formation onboard the ISS using the 40Pb-60Sn solders from the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI), 2) Investigating the effects of elevated and cryogenic temperature conditions in space on solder properties. Considering a range of potential applications and materials, three solder alloys were investigated, including the ISSI lead-based (40Pb-60Sn) solders, off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn solders, and lead-free (95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu) solders, which had recently shown promise for high-performance joint applications due to their good thermal and electrical conductivities, as well as excellent corrosion and fatigue resistance.

Our team conducted the microstructural characterization of four microgravity-processed solders from the ISSI study, one ISSI terrestrial solder, and a third set of freshly made terrestrial 40wt%Pb60wt%Sn solder to demonstrate the effects of the absence of buoyancy and natural convection on void formation in microgravity. The effect of void-induced Marangoni convection on the solder microstructure was demonstrated using the microgravity wire-feed solder. Major Goals/Objectives

The major focus of this project was to elucidate the fundamental mechanisms, phenomenology, and process conditions that govern the integrity and performance of solder joints produced in terrestrial vs. reduced gravity environments, such as the microgravity conditions onboard the International Space Station (ISS). The primary objectives included advancing the current qualitative understanding of porosity formation and persistence in solder joints into the realm of alloy/process-specific quantitative description and prediction and evaluating the influence of elevated and cryogenic temperatures on the microstructural and mechanical properties of solder joints, with emphasis on Sn-based alloys.

Leveraging solder samples from the In-Space Soldering Investigation (ISSI) and other non-ISSI compositions, the project employed a combination of advanced experimental techniques and computational modeling. These approaches were designed to characterize the impacts of voidinduced microstructural variations, extreme thermal cycling, and phase transformations, addressing critical reliability challenges for soldering in space environments. The project aimed to address critical scientific gaps related to solder joint reliability in the unique microgravity and thermal conditions of space, with the ultimate goal of providing quantitative insights for designing more robust soldering techniques. While this proposal focused on understanding the fundamental phenomena, it also laid a solid scientific foundation for future advancements in space fabrication and repair technologies. Project Motivation

Metal joining (welding, brazing, and soldering) in the space environment provides a solution towards sustainable, flexible missions through on-demand fabrication and repair of sustained damage to the spacecraft, satellites, and habitat structures [1, 2]. Metal joining in space is subjected to: a) reduced gravity, b) reduced pressure, and c) a large temperature gradient than terrestrial metal joining. Once the metal joints are produced, they experience extreme temperature variations such as – 120ºC to +25ºC for Mars missions, – 230ºC to +120ºC for the missions to Moon, and – 157ºC to +121ºC outside the ISS. Understanding the metal joining parameters in microgravity and joint integrity during welding, brazing, and soldering under extreme temperatures in space is critical for the safety and success of NASA’s space exploration missions to and beyond low Earth orbit. In this proposed research, we primarily focus on (microgravity vs. terrestrial) solder joints because: ● Solder alloys are

Project Motivation

Solder joints in electronic components are routinely subjected to large temperature variations in the space environment. To compensate, long-duration missions such as Mars rover missions have traditionally kept their electronics in a heated enclosure known as a “warm electronics box” (WEB) so that they do not get exposed to temperature ranges beyond –40ºC to +40ºC [3]. This approach of protecting electronics from extreme temperatures reduces the spacecraft payload ratio, increases launch costs, and fails to protect the electronics, such as solar arrays, exposed outside. Therefore, future missions are planning to use a distributed, non-heated architecture for the rover and spacecraft electronics, where the components will be placed near the systems they interact with rather than in a heated enclosure [4]. This new approach relies on low-cost, commercially available, and space-qualified electronic packaging assemblies. With this approach, electronic components, without requiring heater

Project Motivation

Addressing the reliability of solder joints under these multi-extreme environments is critical for the success of future deep space exploration missions. Specifically, the solder joints used in onboard electronics must be able to withstand elevated and cryogenic temperatures and large variations in temperature. For example, the ISS orbits Earth 16 times in 24 hours and experiences 16 sunsets and sunrises, due to which anything on the outer surface of the ISS experiences extreme cryo and elevated temperature 16 times in a day.

Scientific Questions and Problem Statement

The first year of this project focused on understanding the factors contributing to increased void accumulation in solder joints prepared under microgravity conditions, specifically the higher number and larger size of voids. For a detailed discussion of these findings, refer to the Year 1 report. Building on this foundation, the second year of the study shifted focus toward assessing the reliability of these solder joints in space environments.  
Solder joints are crucial in electronic packaging, serving as mechanical and electrical connectors between components and substrates. A single failure in these solder joints can lead to the malfunction of the integrated circuit or even the entire device. Notably, solder joint failures are the

primary cause of 70% of onboard electronic failures attributed to package failure [7-9]. Therefore, to address the solder joint’s reliability, this project focuses on the following question: _How do extreme temperatures, both elevated and cryogenic, experienced by the solder joint in space affect its properties?_  
Under Cryogenic Temperature:  
- Sn-based solders undergo a ductile to brittle transition (DBT) at the cryo temperature leading to brittle crack formation, which can cause the catastrophic failure of the solder joints.
IOWA STATE UNIVERSITY
Scientific Questions and Problem Statement

- Sn-based solders generally occur a β-Sn to α-Sn phase transition below 13ºC where β- structure (Body-centered tetragonal) transforms to α-structure (Diamond cubic). This phase transformation causes a 26% increase in volume that generates internal stresses, due to which the reliability of the Sn-based solder joints is compromised for space applications. Although there is existing literature on this subject [5, 6, 10], a comprehensive understanding of how these phase transformations influence the solder properties remains elusive.
IOWA STATE UNIVERSITY
Scientific Questions and Problem Statement

The β-Sn to α-Sn transformation is influenced by several factors, including grain size, the presence of specific solutes, and seeding with compatible materials. Coarser grain structures, characterized by fewer heterogeneous nucleation sites such as grain boundaries, corners, and edges, exhibit slower transformation rates. Elements like Pb, Bi, and Sb, which have good solubility in Sn, hinder the transformation by pinning dislocations within the Sn matrix, making lattice expansion energetically unfavorable. In contrast, seeding with materials like α-Sn, InSb, and CdTe, which possess similar lattice parameters, accelerates nucleation and promotes the transformation process [5, 6, 11-15]. Additionally, the finer grains tend to lower the DBTT, while coarser grains raise it. Finer grains provide more grain boundaries, which act as obstacles to crack propagation. Cracks have to change direction repeatedly as they traverse the grain boundaries, requiring more energy and delaying brittle
IOWA STATE UNIVERSITY
Scientific Questions and Problem Statement

to crack propagation. Cracks have to change direction repeatedly as they traverse the grain boundaries, requiring more energy and delaying brittle fracture. This helps maintain ductile behavior to lower temperatures, reducing the DBTT [16]. The solder microstructure in a microgravity environment generally exhibits coarser features compared to those formed under terrestrial conditions. This coarsening is primarily due to the altered dynamics of heat
IOWA STATE UNIVERSITY
Scientific Questions and Problem Statement

and mass transfer in the absence of gravitydriven natural convection. Without buoyancy forces, fluid motion is significantly reduced, and heat transfer relies predominantly on diffusion, which is much slower. Consequently, the slower cooling rates allow grains and phases to grow larger, resulting in a coarser microstructure. As a result, the kinetics of the β-Sn to α-Sn transformation are expected to slow down in microgravity, while the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT) is likely to increase. Results from the ISSI experiments performed aboard the ISS have shown that soldering in microgravity is expected to be considerably different than their ground-based counterparts due to Earth's natural convective flow and buoyancy effects being minimized in microgravity during melting and solidification [21-23]. On Earth, tests showed the solder melting, sagging, dropping, or running down the test wire due to the buoyancy (density) effect (Fig. 2a). In comparison, aboard the ISS, the molten solder was observed to form an equilibrium "football" shape (Fig. 2b). The changes in geometric shape are believed to be due to the dominance of surface tension in microgravity [24-26]. Shortly after equilibrium, the accrued flux was seen spinning around the  
19
IOWA STATE UNIVERSITY
Research Impact/Earth Benefits

sample's surface. As the solder started melting, the internal core of flux was released. When the solder was nearly melted, the released flux formed a drop and migrated to the bottom of the solder, which was closest to the heat source (soldering iron). Shortly after, the flux droplet started to spin around the molten solder. The rotation rate increased steadily and then reached a plateau. This spinning continued until the heat source was removed, after which the flux drop slowed down and eventually stopped. The variation in flux rotation in three samples was probably because of different temperature gradients imposed by different soldering iron tip positions on Cu wire. Also, under typical soldering conditions, rapid reflow temperatures results in flux volatilization and bubble formation. In the presence of gravity, liquid solders tend to mix vigorously during the reflow period due to natural convection. This is beneficial, as any voids or bubbles that form due to evaporated fluxes are quickly swept to free surfaces and are thus removed from the solder joint. However, the situation is worse in the reduced gravity environment of space ( ̴1×10<sup>-5</sup> g) where, due to minimized buoyancy, bubbles have less chance to escape, thus complicating any in-space fabrication and repair operations. The ISSI data has demonstrated that in the _absence_ of gravity, fluid motion is greatly reduced, driven mainly by solidification volume change, thermally induced density gradients, and Marangoni effects. Therefore, due to the lack of buoyancy force and slower mixing in the absence of natural convection, voids, and bubbles are not swept away and become entrapped

due to the lack of buoyancy force and slower mixing in the absence of natural convection, voids, and bubbles are not swept away and become entrapped in the interior of the solder joint upon solidification in microgravity conditions (Fig. 2c vs. d). During the process of soldering, the liquid solder temperature near the substrate, which is in contact with the heater, is higher than that far away from the substrate/heater. Therefore, a distinct surface tension gradient will form with low surface tension in the high-temperature region and high surface tension in the low-temperature region. The effect of such a temperature gradient is predominant in the absence of the buoyancy force and natural convective flow [27]. Then the Marangoni force will tend to pull the voids towards the high-temperature regions such as the substrate.

Long-duration space exploration missions such as Mars rover missions have traditionally kept their electronics in a heated enclosure known as a "warm electronics box" (WEB) to protect them from the extreme cryo temperature on Mars [3]. However, future Mars missions are planning to use a distributed, non-heated architecture for the rover's electronics, where the components will be placed near the systems they interact with rather than in a heated enclosure [3]. This analysis highlights the importance of understanding localized deformation in solder joints under cryogenic conditions, which is crucial for in-space applications. Depending on the soldering environment (microgravity vs. gravity), solder composition, soldering process parameters, and solder microstructure, the solder behavior can vary under cryogenic temperatures. Such as, The absence of natural convection and reduced fluid motion in microgravity results in a coarser grain structure compared to terrestrial conditions, leading to fewer nucleation sites for the β-Sn to α-Sn transformation and slower phase transformation kinetics. However, the coarser grain structure in microgravity is expected to accelerate the ductile-to-brittle transition due to faster transformation kinetics. To mitigate these effects, the addition of trace alloying elements such as indium, bismuth, and silver can help prevent the β-to-α Sn transformation, while rapid cooling can refine the grain structure,

Summary:  
- This study investigated the 40Pb-60Sn solder sample prepared during in-space soldering investigation in microgravity conditions onboard ISS and terrestrial conditions at NASA Marshall, along with solder samples prepared in Dr. Pathak's lab at Iowa State University Ames (ISU). This study also extended to non-ISSI solders such as off-eutectic 50Pb-50Sn and 95.5Sn-3.8Ag-0.7Cu solders prepared in terrestrial conditions at ISU.  
- The effects of microgravity on solder joint formation, microstructure, and mechanical behavior was investigated using advanced characterization techniques. Non-destructive 3D tomography revealed that larger voids occurred only in microgravity due to the absence of natural convection. A quantitative framework demonstrated that ISSI microgravity 40Pb-60Sn wire wrap solder had ~13× more voids than ISSI terrestrial 40Pb-60Sn solder, while ISSI 40Pb60Sn wire feed solder had 4× more voids than ISSI 40Pb-60Sn wire wrap solder.

- The study examined Marangoni convection in microgravity, which induced Pb-rich dendrite accumulation in hot regions, lowering hardness (0.11 GPa) at hot sites compared to colder sites (0.15 GPa). Aging studies on terrestrial 40Pb-60Sn and terrestrial 50Pb-50Sn solder showed grain coarsening and hardness reduction, affecting long-term reliability.

- Cryogenic investigations using in-situ SEM micropillar compression a ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT) in solder. In 40Pb-60Sn, strength increased from 45.9 MPa at RT to 161.4 MPa at -145°C, contradicting the expected β-to-α phase transformation. Additionally, XRD analysis showed no phase transformation. Furthermore, plastic strain dropped from 0.109 at RT to 0.062 at -85°C, saturating below this temperature, with deformation localized at Pb-Sn phase boundaries, confirming DBT.

Strength increased significantly, with instability stress rising from 78.1 MPa at RT to 153 MPa at -145°C.

In contrast, Group 2a, with a mix of Sn-rich and eutectic phases, retained some plasticity, resulting in a more gradual transition.

**1. Overview**

The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is one of six independent experiments that make up the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project for which tests are conducted within the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station (ISS).  
The experiment’s Principal Investigator (PI) is Prof. James G. Quintiere of the <u>Department of Fire Protection Engineering</u> at the University of Maryland.  The experiment has two Co-Investigators (Co-Is), namely Prof. Peter B. Sunderland, of the same U. Maryland department, and Dr. John L. de Ris (FM Global, retired). **2. Science Overview**

##### **A. Background**  
_This background is the Executive Summary from the experiment’s Science Requirements Document (SRD) of June 2013._  
The goal of this research is to establish the burning conditions possible in a microgravity quiescent environment.  The approach is to do this using a burner to emulate (BRE, Burning Rate Emulator) the burning for real condensed fuels, representative of common liquids and solids.  This will be done for quasi-steady burning conditions, albeit ideal in some cases, but the BRE will range over a wide spectrum of real fuel properties.  The key properties governing steady burning are (1) the heat of gasification, (2) the surface re-radiation heat flux, and (3) the heat of combustion.  Flame radiation is also relevant in general and can be represented in terms of the laminar smoke point. Its importance in microgravity flames needs study, but the first three properties are key.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

Currently NASA assesses the flammability hazard of materials for use in space flight by an upward flame spread “pass-fail” test (Test 1), and supplements with data from the Cone Calorimeter (Test 2).  The latter test has the capability of measuring the three properties listed above.  Hence, the successful application of the BRE in microgravity can enhance the usefulness of Test 2.  
Fundamental and ad hoc testing in microgravity at quiescent conditions has shown that quasisteady flames can be supported on candle-wicks, droplets, jets and, at very low ambient velocities, small plastic samples and a burner flame.  The established flames tend to have spherical or semi-

**2. Science Overview**

Gas burners like the BRE have been used to successfully simulate burning of a wide range of fuels in terms of their _B_ numbers and configurations over a range of Grashof numbers.  We have successfully shown that for planar burning at different angle orientations that a burner can emulate the flame standoff distribution, and even match the onset of unsteadiness to turbulent flow.  Theoretical analyses of such a problem are limited by the inability to accurately deal with flame radiation, turbulence and variable properties.  A burner simulation can be far superior as it inherently contains these effects.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

The construction of a 50 mm diameter prototype BRE burner with flame heat flux sensors has enabled us to emulate both a methanol and heptane pool fire of the 50 mm diameter, reproducing its color, flame character and shape, and heat of gasification for nearly the same surface temperatures.  We show that the BRE is capable of displaying the burning conditions in terms of the fuel properties of heat of combustion, heat of gasification, and surface re-radiant heat flux (with some likely effect of smoke point).  A preliminary 3-D plot of steady burning gives a flammability mapping in terms of these variables under conditions of gravity and atmospheric variations.  A mapping in microgravity can demonstrate the burning conditions for a wide range of real materials in terms of these properties.  In addition the effect of external radiation can indirectly be assessed.  The 50 mm burner has been redesigned, along with a 25 mm burner, to reduce edge effects, provide improved heat flux sensors

**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

The primary objective is to observe the burning behavior (including extinction) in long-duration microgravity for methane/nitrogen and ethylene/nitrogen mixtures on a porous circular burner of 25 and 50 mm diameter at various pressures, ambient oxygen, and CO2 (desired, to assess extinguishment).  Ignition will not be directly studied in microgravity studies, as we believe normal-gravity experiments are sufficient for its study.  Another objective is to obtain conditions that can be related to microgravity behavior of condensed fuels that embrace the scope of real liquid and solid fuels.  
We think these results can establish fuel properties that directly relate to the fire hazard in spacecraft, and these properties can be derived from NASA Test 2.  The BRE is an efficient, safe, and comprehensive technique for achieving these results.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

This version of the Science Requirements Document has been refined since the Science Concept Review (Aug 28, 2012).  The panel wrote at that time that they “strongly encourage continued development of the BRE experiment for implementation into the ACME and testing on the ISS.” We have tried to address most of their recommendations and suggestions.  In addition, work has progressed to include the development of two papers, and the commencement of drop facility testing of the BRE.  Those results have shown quasi-steady flames, and are very encouraging.

##### **B. Rationale for Microgravity**  
_This is the ‘Justification for Extended Duration Microgravity’ section (2.5) of the experiment’s SRD from June 2013.  Equations are not included here, but they can be found in the SRD._
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

Fire in a spacecraft microgravity environment is a likely event based on limited accident data, tests to burn materials, and research that has explored simple burning scenarios.  Indeed, NASA screens the use of materials on spacecraft by its flammability Test 1.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

Currently NASA Test 1 and Test 2 are incapable of directly analyzing material fire hazards in spacecraft. There is no predictive methodology to extrapolate from these tests.  However, NASA Test 2, the Cone Calorimeter, is capable of determining heats of combustion and gasification, and surface reradiation in burning. Steady (or quasi-steady) burning rate data from the BRE in flight experiments will establish a flammability mapping in terms of these properties for microgravity. In addition, using Eq. (2), the results can establish the necessary heat flux condition for other fuels to burn in microgravity.  The BRE is an efficient way to achieve quasi-steady burning. While microgravity tests of condensed fuels have been performed and are planned, they are limited in their ability to reveal sufficient information about the diverse condensed fuels that exist aboard the ISS.  Moreover the time to achieve quasi-steady burning rate of solid fuels can be of the order of minutes as dictated by
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

fuels that exist aboard the ISS.  Moreover the time to achieve quasi-steady burning rate of solid fuels can be of the order of minutes as dictated by the time response of the solid.  The BRE can be turned on and off quickly, and its quasi-steady condition is only dependent on the gas phase phenomenon.  While this time is shorter, it can still be on the order of 10 seconds or more.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

The proposed tests cannot be performed in parabolic aircraft owing to considerable g-jitter disturbances.  While limited testing is possible in drop facilities, the characteristic times for the gas phase (approximately 20 s) and the burner surface temperature (approximately 40 s) preclude consideration of quasi-steady conditions.  Preliminary testing in the NASA 5.2 s drop facility indicated the approach to quasi-steady burning, but longer tests are needed to confirm this tendency.  The longer duration testing in the ISS with the efficient operation of the BRE can produce results only limited by the gas-phase response time.  
##### **C. Science Objectives**  
_The proposed objectives text presented here is the ‘Experimental Objectives’ section (2.2) of the experiment’s SRD from June 2013.  ISS testing was not carried out to address the desired second objective, where NASA effectively limited this experiment to the first and third objectives._
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**2. Science Overview**

The BRE flight program seeks to establish the burning conditions in a quiescent microgravity ambient in terms of material properties.  The specific flight objectives are as follows.  
1. Observe burning behavior in long-duration microgravity for CH4/N2 and C2H4/N2 mixtures on porous circular burners of 25 and 50 mm diameter.  Consider O2/N2 ambients with various pressures and ambient O2 concentrations and pressures.  NASAconsidered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.  Emphasize fuel conditions that can be related to a diverse range of condensed fuels.  
2. Consider the conditions of Objective 1 for ambients of O2/CO2 (desired).  
3. Consider the conditions of Objectives 1 – 2 for extinction limits.

ACME’s chamber insert, which is ~0.4 m in diameter, provides common mounting for a variety of burners on the chamber axis (but only one at a time) and includes a retracting resistive igniter.  As depicted in Figure 3, there will initially be gas-jet burners (with inner diameters ranging from 0.4 to 3.2 mm), a small coflow burner (where the two concentric tubes have inner diameters of 2.1 and 25 mm), porous spherical burners (with diameters ranging from 6.35 to 12.7 mm), and two flat porous burners for the BRE experiment (with inner diameters of 25 and 50 mm).  Most burners will be equipped with a surface thermocouple, and each BRE burner will have two heat flux transducers.  The internal pressure of the porous burners will be measured to allow monitoring of the pressure differential across the outlet surface.  The igniter will have a crew-exchangeable tip and arm (to accommodate the various burners) and its stepper-motor drive will allow for precise positioning.

Color imaging is provided by two cameras: a high-definition digital camera mounted outside of the chamber and a standard analog camera mounted on the chamber insert (with a turning mirror). The burner has shown that quasi-steady burning is possible for real solids with a flat surface of 25 mm diameter.  Up to now most flammability studies in microgravity have focused on flame spread with a wind for concurrent spread and at least a self-induced wind for opposed flow spread.  We already knew that this would be possible from normal-gravity research.  The burning of liquids, as in a wick of a candle flame and small droplets, has been shown to produce steady flames.  However, many droplet flames were found to extinguish owing to radiative cooling of the flame.  We see this as well in the extended ISS microgravity tests. However, this extinction was predominately seen for nominal ambient conditions of 21% oxygen and 14.7 psia.  At conditions of 27% oxygen, 10.2 psia and 34% oxygen, 8.2 psia, the flames generally persisted for 3 minutes or more.  These are all atmospheric conditions that NASA is considering for future spacecraft.

##### **D. Surprises and New Discoveries**  
Initial surprises and discoveries include:  
- (1) It is found out that quasi-steady burning on a flat surface, representing a pool fire, can exist in microgravity. Ambient oxygen mole fraction plays the most significant role in this regard. The quasi-steady flames were observed for nominal ambient oxygen mole fractions of 0.265 and above.  
- (2) Although ambient pressure has a weak effect on the quality of burning, it affects radiative heat loss by changing the partial pressures of radiating species, i.e., H2O and CO2.  
- (3) Methane nitrogen-generated flames self-extinguished within a minute for all ambient conditions.  That indicates that the burn time depends on the fuel chemistry.  
- (4) Ethylene flames, which tend to soot under normal gravity conditions, did not soot under microgravity conditions. Sooting only occurred upon ignition and disappeared quickly after ignition.  Nitrogen dilution reduced the amount of soot.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**4. Preliminary Results**

- (5) Radiative loss fraction for the flames in microgravity can reach about 60% compared to 30% for the normal gravity flames.  
- (6) TFP measurements of four flames confirmed that critical temperature range for extinction is 1100 to 1200 K.  This is confirmed by numerical simulations.  
- (7) A It was shown that the BRE can emulate several liquids and solids including Acetone, Ethanol, Methanol, PMMA, Nylon, Phenolic glass fiber, etc. as demonstrated by a flammability diagram, as a plot of heats of gasification vs. the mass burning rate, based on the steady average surface heat flux.  
- (8) For the first time, two limits of extinction were obtained on a plot of heat of combustion vs. heats of gasification.  The plot shows the flammability region for each nominal ambient oxygen mole fraction with radiative extinction for large flames and another extinction limit for small flames.

##### **F. Additional Objectives Achieved**  
An empirical correlation for the radiative loss fraction was obtained through a dimensional analysis of the radiation data.  The correlation was used to predict the flames’ radiative loss fractions from their mass burning rate, oxygen mole fraction in the ambient, chamber pressure, and heat of combustion.  This result was used to correct the heat of combustion in the analytical solution for these flames.

**4. Preliminary Results**

##### **G. Impacts, Benefits, and Products**  
BRE yielded important data relevant to spacecraft fire safety.  Quasi-steady burning corresponding to various condensed-phase materials (such as PMMA and Nylon) was observed in microgravity despite the absence of air flow, where the cessation of ventilation is an established step in putting out spacecraft fires.  The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.  
While BRE’s results are still preliminary, they suggest that NASA may want to increase use of its alternative flammability Test 2, with the cone calorimeter, where that test can measure material properties corresponding to the microgravity flames observed with the BRE burner.

The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.  More specifically, BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.  A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.  A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are

##### **A. Discussion of Method/Protocol**  
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests. All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the Glenn ISS Payload Operations Center (GIPOC). All of the first round of tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen.  The tests were carried out at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats.  More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.  In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests.

BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment, but the tests are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is highly sooting because of its carbon double bond.  Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen was premixed on the ground prior to launch for some cases.  But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.

###### **2. Any other difficulties in obtaining scientific data**  
BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often saturated.  Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.  Estimates had been made of the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the radiometers.  As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity.  The estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been sufficiently tracked in the hardware development.  Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60

Ignition was not always successful, where BRE tests were sometimes conducted under conditions, e.g., for igniter activation and deactivation, which led to momentary flashes without sustained ignition.  Given that unplanned crew time is required to replace failed igniter tips, the BRE ops team limited - to varying degrees - the igniter voltage and the time that it was energized within the flame.  The latter was known from earlier research in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) to degrade the hot-wire igniter tip and hasten its demise.  It is notable that the flashes of flame (across the burner surface) sometimes continued briefly after the igniter was deactivated and retracted.  In one case on the first day of testing, there was excess fuel and a ‘fireball’ was ignited which promptly quenched. #### **I. Introduction**  
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.  More specifically, BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.  A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.  A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are

##### **A. Discussion of Method/Protocol**  
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.

All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the NASA Glenn Research Center.  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it may alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.  For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady data has been collected.  But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far for BRE or ACME in general.  
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.  
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

#### **III. Results**  
##### **A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight**  
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, where a total of 45 flames were ignited during Increment 58.  That round was completed in April 2019, during the beginning of Increment 59, when an additional 17 flames were ignited.  As such, a total of 62 flames were ignited in the first round of testing.  Meanwhile, the second round of BRE testing is expected to begin near the end of Increment 61 and continue into Increment 62.  The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.

**30-day Operational Accomplishments Report**

All of the first round of tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen.  The tests were carried out at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats.  More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen.  In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests.  An exception is tests conducted after the chamber atmosphere was vented and refilled, such as the first test of the day.  But the atmosphere was typically refreshed once during each of testing.

BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often saturated.  Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.  Estimates had been made of the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the radiometers.  As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity.  The estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been sufficiently tracked in the hardware development.  Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60 times the duration of the drop tests. The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from the flame to the burner surface.  In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated fuel.  The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix).  Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity.  Other than for a candle flame, this has not been shown before.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**30-day Operational Accomplishments Report**

The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface. One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center.  The resulting data suffered from two possible effects.   The first effect is the condensation of water vapor.  As the sensors are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor.  This occurs, as the dew point for combustion products is about 60-70<sup>o</sup> C, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature and can achieve temperatures over 100<sup>o</sup> C.  Thus, condensation can occur at temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor.  Above the dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor.

The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.  More specifically, BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.  A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.  A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and alcohol by matching properties including the heats of combustion and

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are

With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application.

#### **II. Methods/Research Operations**  
##### **A. Discussion of Method/Protocol**  
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.  
All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the NASA Glenn Research Center.  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in

For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady data has been collected.  But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far for BRE or ACME in general.

The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of 45 flames were ignited. The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.  However, the break was longer than had been planned because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew availability.  As a result, BRE’s second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds of the preceding ACME experiment, Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), was completed, where that occurred in July 2020.  A factor in that decision was the delayed start of commercial crew launches and understanding that crew availability would be limited until such crew launches entered an operational, rather than demonstration, phase.

More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen.  In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with nitrogen and any incomplete combustion products (e.g., water vapor and carbon dioxide) from preceding tests. BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting because of its carbon double bond.  Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen were premixed on the ground prior to launch for some cases.  But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.

BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often saturated.  Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.  Estimates had been made of the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the radiometers.  As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity.  The estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been sufficiently tracked in the hardware development.  Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60 times the duration of the drop tests.  With the fixed amplification of the radiometer signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were

The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated fuel.  The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix).  Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity. Other than for a candle flame, this has not been shown before.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**30-day Operational Accomplishments Report**

The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface. One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center ( _r_ = 9.5 mm). As the sensors are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor.  This occurs, as the dew point for combustion products is about 60-70<sup>o</sup> C, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature and can achieve temperatures over 100<sup>o</sup> C.   Thus, condensation can occur at temperatures below the dew point that leads to added heat to the sensor.  Above the dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor.  When the sensor is dry and above 100<sup>o</sup> C, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases as intended.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**30-day Operational Accomplishments Report**

The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water fully evaporates.  More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect.  Fortunately, by the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone.

#### **I. Introduction**  
The Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) experiment is conducted in the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) on the International Space Station, as part of the Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) project.  BRE is focused on spacecraft fire prevention.  More specifically, BRE’s goals are to improve our fundamental understanding of materials flammability, such as extinction behavior and the conditions needed for sustained combustion, and to assess the relevance of existing flammability test methods for low and partial-gravity environments.  A flat porous burner fed with gaseous fuel simulates the burning of solid and liquid fuels, where measurements are made of the thermal feedback (i.e., to the burner) upon which the vaporization of condensed-phase fuels is dependent.  A small number of gaseous fuels (including mixtures with inert gases) are used to simulate the burning of fuels such as paper, plastic, and

Microgravity studies of flames allow for a range of simplifications and provide various advantages over normal-gravity studies.  For example, the flicker of flame, which is a buoyancy-driven (i.e., gravity-driven) instability, is eliminated yielding quasi-steady flames in microgravity.  Length scales are increased in microgravity flames facilitating analysis of the flame structure. Momentum-dominated flames, which are important for most practical combustion, can be studied at low velocities to simplify analysis.  Microgravity flames tend to have a much stronger sensitivity to their atmosphere and exhibit a much broader range of characteristics than normalgravity flames because of the near absence of buoyant entrainment.  The long residence times in microgravity flames can lead to strong soot production, but many microgravity flames are soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are

soot free.  The absence of buoyancy makes microgravity flames advantageous for studies of limit and stability behavior where chemical kinetics are important.  With these advantages, microgravity testing can lead to new understanding of the complex nature of combustion – regardless of the gravitational environment of the combustion application.

#### **II. Methods/Research Operations**  
##### **A. Discussion of Method/Protocol**  
BRE and other ACME experiments are configured, but not conducted, by the ISS crew. The crew’s role is to set up the hardware, gas bottles, etc. for each set of tests.  The most common changes include the gas bottles on the Combustion Integrated Rack (CIR) and the mass flow controllers on the modular ACME chamber insert.

All testing is commanded from the ground, specifically from the operations center at the NASA Glenn Research Center.  The science portion of the testing is typically conducted in a nominally automated mode using pre-programmed scripts.  However, it could alternately be conducted in a ‘manual’ mode, where changes are made to a control parameter in response to the analog video downlink and the numerical data available in the telemetry stream.  For example, gas flow rate(s) can be adjusted after quasi-steady data has been collected.  But testing has not been conducted in a ‘manual’ mode thus far for BRE or ACME in general.  
Testing is not conducted when thrusters fire or spacecraft dock or undock from ISS to ensure an acceptable acceleration environment.  
Data is downlinked between each set of tests, i.e., day of testing, to allow for preliminary analysis and requisite planning for subsequent testing.

#### **III. Results**  
##### **A. Baselined Activities Completed – Pre-flight, In-flight, Post-Flight**  
The first round of BRE tests began in February 2019, during Increment 58, when a total of 45 flames were ignited.  That round was completed in April 2019, during Increment 59, when an additional 17 flames were ignited.  BRE’s second-round flame testing began in Sept. 2020, during Increment 63, in which 47 flames were ignited.  The second and final round of tests was completed in Jan. 2021, during Increment 64, when another 85 flames were ignited.  As a result, 62 and 132 flames were respectively ignited in the first and second rounds of testing for a total of 194 flames.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**30-day Operational Accomplishments Report**

The ‘interruption’ in the BRE testing was intentionally planned years in advance to enable the PI team to review the initial results in detail and with that knowledge plan the second round of tests to maximize its scientific outcome.  However, the break was longer than had been planned because of combination of hardware issues and limited crew availability.  As a result, BRE’s second round was rescheduled to occur after both rounds of the preceding ACME experiment, Structure and Response of Spherical Diffusion Flames (s-Flame), was completed, where that occurred in July 2020.  A factor in that decision was the delayed start of commercial crew launches and understanding that crew availability would be limited until such crew launches entered an operational, rather than demonstration, phase.

All first-round tests were conducted with the 25-mm diameter BRE burner while burning ethylene (C2H4) - sometimes diluted with nitrogen.  The tests were carried out at a range of chamber pressures and oxygen concentrations, generally representative of possible crew environments in future spacecraft or habitats.  More specifically, testing was especially focused on atmospheric conditions at (1) 14.7 psia, 21% oxygen; (2) 10.2 psia, 26.5% oxygen; and (3) 8.2 psia, 34% oxygen.  In all cases, the atmosphere was diluted with

Second round testing was carried out including both BRE burner diameters, i.e., 25 and 50 mm, and on some days with methane (CH4) – again sometimes diluted with nitrogen. Therefore, the second round of tests featured a broader range of conditions than investigated during the first round.  However, in contrast to the first round most of the round 2 tests were carried out at roughly 14.7 psia, although pressure has a secondary effect on flames.  Meanwhile, the tests in this round were carried out at various oxygen concentrations as in the first round but were more often conducted with ~40% oxygen, where oxygen of course has a strong effect on combustion.

BRE does not have living subjects like a life science experiment. The tests are independently conducted with two different gaseous fuels, methane and ethylene.  Both are simple hydrocarbon gases for which the chemistry is well understood.  Methane (CH4) is the primary component of natural gas and tends to produce low levels of soot given the absence of carbon-carbon bonds.  Meanwhile, ethylene (C2H4), is normally highly sooting because of its carbon double bond.  Tests are conducted with pure fuel and fuel mixed with nitrogen, where the fuel and nitrogen were premixed on the ground prior to launch for some cases.  But the ACME hardware also allows for simultaneous flow of fuel and nitrogen to the burner, allowing for on-orbit fuel dilution and testing at a continuum of fuel concentrations.

BRE’s primary problem was that the sensors for measuring the thermal radiation often saturated.  Although the measurements were not required to meet experiment success, they were considered sufficiently critical that BRE was equipped with its own radiometer array, featuring three thermopile detectors.  Estimates had been made of the signal levels based on 5-second drop tests since the hot gases tend to blanket the flame in the absence of buoyancy and thereby remain within the view of the radiometers.  As a result, the signal levels are strongly dependent on gravity.  The estimates were not part of the science requirements and may not have been sufficiently tracked in the hardware development.  Furthermore, the ISS tests lasted as long as 5 minutes, which is over four times the envisioned BRE test duration and 60 times the duration of the drop tests.  With the fixed amplification of the radiometer signals, the data was frequently lost - other than the knowledge that the limits were

All of the round 1 and 2 tests have had the heat flux sensor data reduced using their original calibrations.  As presented below, the data is being processed to address the effect of the combustion product water condensation on the sensor surfaces.  
The primary measurements are used, by two techniques, to obtain the net heat flux from the flame to the burner surface. In the steady state, this net heat flux divided by the mass flow rate per unit area of the fuel mixture gives the heat of gasification of the emulated fuel.  The key hypothesis is that the heat of combustion, smoke point, and heat of gasification of the fuel mixture will represent a real solid fuel (or liquid fuel absorbed in an inert matrix).  Thus, achieved steady burning would represent the potential for real solid fuels to achieve steady burning in microgravity.  Other than for a candle flame, this has not been shown before.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**30-day Operational Accomplishments Report**

The first technique uses two thermopile heat flux gages embedded in the burner surface. One gage is at the center the other is offset from the center ( _r_ = 9.5 mm). As the sensors are not cooled, but rise with temperature as the flame grows, water from its combustion products can condense and then evaporate from the sensor.  This occurs, as the dew point for combustion products is about 60-70<sup>o</sup> C, and the sensor begins at ambient temperature and can achieve temperatures over 100<sup>o</sup> C.  Thus, condensation can occur at temperatures below the dew point that lead to added heat to the sensor.  Above the dew point, the condensed water will evaporate and reduce the heat to the sensor.  When the sensor is dry and above 100<sup>o</sup> C, it will only measure the heat flux from the flame gases as intended.
**Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments (ACME) Burning Rate Emulator (BRE) ACME/BRE Final Report (2022*)**
**30-day Operational Accomplishments Report**

We have duplicated this condensation effect in 1-g laboratory experiments with the duplicative NASA BRE burner.  Fig. 1 illustrates the condensation and evaporation effect in the ISS tests.  The offset sensor in red shows a clear jump increase when the water fully evaporates.  More analysis is needed to properly correct for this effect.  Fortunately, by the end of the test shown here (and for all of the other data), this water effect is gone.

##### **Week 20: February 8-14**  
On GMT 039, we performed our first ACME BRE (Burning Rate Emulator) test points. Unlike the other ACME experiments, BRE is focused on improving spacecraft fire safety rather than practical terrestrial combustion. More specifically, BRE uses gaseous fuels to determine the flammability of liquids and solids in microgravity by selecting test conditions to match key parameters. We performed nine successful tests burning ethylene on the 25-mm diameter burner, where the burner’s embedded sensors measure the heat flux that would normally vaporize a liquid or solid fuel. The tests were conducted under a range of oxygen concentrations and pressures, including some atmospheres that could be used for future crew vehicles or habitats.
